entries.5113786eef6bcc04a8966b50856b66e7a6231548: <div sID="gen32063" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Col.2" sID="Col.2"/> <div eID="gen32063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32064" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32065" type="x-p"/> I. The apostle expresses concern for the Colossians, <reference osisRef="Col.2.1-Col.2.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He repeats it again, <reference osisRef="Col.2.5">ver. 5</reference>. III. He cautions them against false teachers among the Jews (<reference osisRef="Col.2.4">ver. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.2.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.2.7">7</reference>), and against the Gentile philosophy, <reference osisRef="Col.2.8-Col.2.12">ver. 8-12</reference>. IV. He represents the privileges of Christians, <reference osisRef="Col.2.13-Col.2.15">ver. 13-15</reference>. And, V. Concludes with a caution against the judaizing teachers, and those who would introduce the worship of angels, <reference osisRef="Col.2.16-Col.2.23">ver. 16-23</reference>.
entries.3ac4bee5c77bf4840ba612b8a80bc20e5eee71fb: <div eID="gen32065" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32064" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul's Concern for the Colossians. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32066" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> For I would that ye knew what great conflict I have for you, and <hi type="italic">for</hi> them at Laodicea, and <hi type="italic">for</hi> as many as have not seen my face in the flesh; <hi type="super">2</hi> That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ; <hi type="super">3</hi> In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. <div eID="gen32066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32067" type="x-p"/> We may observe here the great concern which Paul had for these Colossians and the other churches which he had not any personal knowledge of. The apostle had never been at Colosse, and the church planted there was not of his planting; and yet he had as tender a care of it as if it had been the only people of his charge (<reference osisRef="Col.2.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">For I would that you knew what great conflict I have for you, and for those at Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in the flesh.</hi> Observe, 1. Paul's care of the church was such as amounted to a conflict. He was in a sort of agony, and had a constant fear respecting what would become of them. Herein he was a follower of his Master, who was in an agony for us, and was <hi type="italic">heard in that he feared.</hi> (2.) We may keep up a communion by faith, hope, and holy love, even with those churches and fellow-christians of whom we have no personal knowledge, and with whom we have no conversation. We can think, and pray, and be concerned for one another, at the greatest distance; and those we never saw in the flesh we may hope to meet in heaven. But, <div eID="gen32067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32068" type="x-p"/> I. What was it that the apostle desired for them? <hi type="italic">That their hearts may be comforted, being knit together in love,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Col.2.2">v. 2</reference>. It was their spiritual welfare about which he was solicitous. He does not say that they may be healthy, and merry, and rich, and great, and prosperous; but that their <hi type="italic">hearts may be comforted.</hi> Note, The prosperity of the soul is the best prosperity, and what we should be most solicitous about for ourselves and others. We have here a description of soul-prosperity. <div eID="gen32068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32069" type="x-p"/> 1. When our knowledge grows to an understanding of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ,—when we come to have a more clear, distinct, methodical knowledge of the truth as it is in Jesus, then the soul prospers: <hi type="italic">To understand the mystery,</hi> either what was before concealed, but is now made known concerning the Father and Christ, or the mystery before mentioned, of calling the Gentiles into the Christian church, as the Father and Christ have revealed it in the gospel; and not barely to speak of it by rote, or as we have been taught it by our catechisms, but to be led into it, and enter into the meaning and design of it. This is what we should labour after, and then the soul prospers. <div eID="gen32069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32070" type="x-p"/> 2. When our faith grows to a full assurance and bold acknowledgment of this mystery. (1.) To a full assurance, or a well-settled judgment, upon their proper evidence, of the great truths of the gospel, without doubting, or calling them in question, but embracing them with the highest satisfaction, as faithful sayings and worthy of all acceptation. (2.) When it comes to a free acknowledgment, and we not only believe with the heart, but are ready, when called to it, to make confession with our mouth, and are not ashamed of our Master and our holy religion, under the frowns and violence of their enemies. This is called the <hi type="italic">riches of the full assurance of understanding.</hi> Great knowledge and strong faith make a soul rich. This is being rich towards God, and rich in faith, and having the true riches, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.21">Luke xii. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.16.11">xvi. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.5">Jam. ii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen32070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32071" type="x-p"/> 3. It consists in the abundance of comfort in our souls: <hi type="italic">That their hearts might be comforted.</hi> The soul prospers when it is filled with joy and peace (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.13">Rom. xv. 13</reference>), and has a satisfaction within which all the troubles without cannot disturb, and is able to joy in the Lord when all other comforts fail, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.17-Hab.3.18">Hab. iii. 17, 18</reference>. <div eID="gen32071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32072" type="x-p"/> 4. The more intimate communion we have with our fellow-christians the more the soul prospers: <hi type="italic">Being knit together in love.</hi> Holy love knits the hearts of Christians one to another; and faith and love both contribute to our comfort. The stronger our faith is, and the warmer our love, the greater will our comfort be. Having occasion to mention Christ (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">v. 2</reference>), according to his usual way, he makes this remark to his honour (<reference osisRef="Col.2.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.</hi> He had said (<reference osisRef="Col.1.19">ch. i. 19</reference>) <hi type="italic">that all fulness dwells in him:</hi> here he mentions particularly the <hi type="italic">treasures of wisdom and knowledge.</hi> There is a fulness of wisdom in him, as he has perfectly revealed the will of God to mankind. Observe, The treasures of wisdom are hidden not from us, but for us, in Christ. Those who would be wise and knowing must make application to Christ. We must spend upon the stock which is laid up for us in him, and draw from the treasures which are hidden in him. He is the wisdom of God, and is <hi type="italic">of God made unto us wisdom,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.24">1 Cor. i. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">30</reference>. <div eID="gen32072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32073" type="x-p"/> II. His concern for them is repeated (<reference osisRef="Col.2.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Though I am absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, joying, and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ.</hi> Observe, 1. We may be present in spirit with those churches and Christians from whom we are absent in body; for the communion of saints is a spiritual thing. Paul had heard concerning the Colossians that they were orderly and regular; and though he had never seen them, nor was present with them, he tells them he could easily think himself among them, and look with pleasure upon their good behaviour. 2. The order and stedfastness of Christians are matter of joy to ministers; they joy when they behold their order, their regular behaviour and stedfast adherence to the Christian doctrine. 3. The more stedfast our faith in Christ is, the better order there will be in our whole conversation; for we live and walk by faith, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.7">2 Cor. v. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">Heb. x. 38</reference>.
entries.80d39ff967fc4b94bb27ca9ac666e970d493c2fb: <div eID="gen32073" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Glory of the Christian Economy. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32074" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And this I say, lest any man should beguile you with enticing words. <hi type="super">5</hi> For though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ. <hi type="super">6</hi> As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, <hi type="italic">so</hi> walk ye in him: <hi type="super">7</hi> Rooted and built up in him, and stablished in the faith, as ye have been taught, abounding therein with thanksgiving. 8 Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ. <hi type="super">9</hi> For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. <hi type="super">10</hi> And ye are complete in him, which is the head of all principality and power: <hi type="super">11</hi> In whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ: <hi type="super">12</hi> Buried with him in baptism, wherein also ye are risen with <hi type="italic">him</hi> through the faith of the operation of God, who hath raised him from the dead. <div eID="gen32074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32075" type="x-p"/> The apostle cautions the Colossians against deceivers (<reference osisRef="Col.2.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">And this I say lest any man beguile you with enticing words;</hi> and <reference osisRef="Col.2.8">v. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">Lest any man spoil you.</hi> He insists so much upon the perfection of Christ and the gospel revelation, to preserve them from the ensnaring insinuations of those who would corrupt their principles. Note, 1. The way in which Satan spoils souls is by beguiling them. He deceives them, and by this means slays them. He is the <hi type="italic">old serpent who beguiled Eve through his subtlety,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.3">2 Cor. xi. 3</reference>. He could not ruin us if he did not cheat us; and he could not cheat us but by our own fault and folly. 2. Satan's agents, who aim to spoil them, beguile them with enticing words. See the danger of enticing words; how many are ruined by the flattery of those who lie in wait to deceive, and by the false disguises and fair appearances of evil principles and wicked practices. <hi type="italic">By good words, and fair speeches, they deceive the hearts of the simple,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.16.18">Rom. xvi. 18</reference>. "You ought to stand upon your guard against enticing words, and be aware and afraid of those who would entice you to any evil; for that which they aim at is to spoil you." <hi type="italic">If sinners entice thee, consent thou not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.10">Prov. i. 10</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen32075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32076" type="x-p"/> I. A sovereign antidote against seducers (<reference osisRef="Col.2.6-Col.2.7">v. 6, 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">As you have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk you in him, rooted and built up,</hi> &c. Here note, 1. All Christians have, in profession at least, <hi type="italic">received Jesus Christ the Lord,</hi> received him as Christ, the great prophet of the church, anointed by God to reveal his will; as Jesus the great high priest, and Saviour from sin and wrath, by the expiatory sacrifice of himself; and as Lord, or sovereign and king, whom we are to obey and be subject to.—<hi type="italic">Received him,</hi> consented to him, taken him for ours in every relation and every capacity, and for all the purposes and uses of them. 2. The great concern of those who have received Christ is <hi type="italic">to walk in him</hi>—to make their practices conformable to their principles and their conversation agreeable to their engagements. As we have received Christ, or consented to be his, so we must walk with him in our daily course and keep up our communion with him. 3. The more closely we walk with Christ the more we are <hi type="italic">rooted and established in the faith.</hi> A good conversation is the best establishment of a good faith. If we walk in him, we shall be rooted in him; and the more firmly we are rooted in him the more closely we shall walk in him: <hi type="italic">Rooted and built up.</hi> Observe, We cannot be built up in Christ, unless we be first rooted in him. We must be united to him by a lively faith, and heartily consent to his covenant, and then we shall <hi type="italic">grow up in him in all things.</hi>—<hi type="italic">As you have been taught</hi>—"according to the rule of the Christian doctrine, in which you have been instructed." Observe, A good education has a good influence upon our establishment. We must be <hi type="italic">established in the faith, as we have been taught, abounding therein.</hi> Observe, Being established in the faith, we must abound therein, and improve in it more and more; and this with thanksgiving. The way to have the benefit and comfort of God's grace is to be much in giving thanks for it. We must join thanksgiving to all our improvements, and be sensible of the mercy of all our privileges and attainments. Observe, <div eID="gen32076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32077" type="x-p"/> II. The fair warning given us of our danger: <hi type="italic">Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.2.8">v. 8</reference>. There is a philosophy which is a noble exercise of our reasonable faculties, and highly serviceable to religion, such a study of the works of God as leads us to the knowledge of God and confirms our faith in him. But there is a philosophy which is vain and deceitful, which is prejudicial to religion, and sets up the wisdom of man in competition with the wisdom of God, and while it pleases men's fancies ruins their faith; as nice and curious speculations about things above us, or of no use and concern to us; or a care of words and terms of art, which have only an empty and often a cheating appearance of knowledge. <hi type="italic">After the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world:</hi> this plainly reflects upon the Jewish pedagogy or economy, as well as the Pagan learning. The Jews governed themselves by the traditions of their elders and the rudiments or elements of the world, the rites and observances which were only preparatory and introductory to the gospel state; the Gentiles mixed their maxims of philosophy with their Christian principles; and both alienated their minds from Christ. Those who pin their faith on other men's sleeves, and walk in the way of the world, have turned away from following after Christ. The deceivers were especially the Jewish teachers, who endeavoured to keep up the law of Moses in conjunction with the gospel of Christ, but really in competition with it and contradiction to it. Now here the apostle shows, <div eID="gen32077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32078" type="x-p"/> 1. That we have in Christ the substance of all the shadows of the ceremonial law; for example, (1.) Had they then the Shechinah, or special presence of God, called the glory, from the visible token of it? So have we now in Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Col.2.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.</hi> Under the law, the presence of God dwelt between the cherubim, in a cloud which covered the mercy-seat; but now it dwells in the person of our Redeemer, who partakes of our nature, and is bone of our bone and flesh of our flesh, and has more clearly declared the Father to us. It dwells in him bodily; not as the body is opposed to the spirit, but as the body is opposed to the shadow. The fulness of the Godhead dwells in the Christ really, and not figuratively; for he is both God and man. (2.) Had they circumcision, which was the seal of the covenant? In Christ we are <hi type="italic">circumcised with the circumcision made without hands</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.2.11">v. 11</reference>), by the work of regeneration in us, which is the spiritual or Christian circumcision. <hi type="italic">He is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Rom. ii. 29</reference>. This is owing to Christ, and belongs to the Christian dispensation. <hi type="italic">It is made without hands;</hi> not by the power of any creature, but by the power of the blessed Spirit of God. We are <hi type="italic">born of the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.5">John iii. 5</reference>. And it is <hi type="italic">the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.3.5">Tit. iii. 5</reference>. It consists <hi type="italic">in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh,</hi> in renouncing sin and reforming our lives, not in mere external rites. It is not the <hi type="italic">putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience towards God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.21">1 Pet. iii. 21</reference>. And it is not enough to put away some one particular sin, but we must put off the whole body of sin. The <hi type="italic">old man must be crucified, and the body of sin destroyed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.6.6">Rom. vi. 6</reference>. Christ was circumcised, and, by virtue of our union to him, we partake of that effectual grace which puts off the <hi type="italic">body of the sins of the flesh.</hi> Again, The Jews thought themselves complete in the ceremonial law; but we are <hi type="italic">complete in Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.2.10">v. 10</reference>. That was imperfect and defective; <hi type="italic">if the first covenant had been faultless, there would no place have been sought for the second</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.7">Heb. viii. 7</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">law was but a shadow of good things, and could never, by those sacrifices, make the comers thereunto perfect,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.1">Heb. x. 1</reference>. But all the defects of it are made up in the gospel of Christ, by the complete sacrifice for sin and revelation of the will of God. <hi type="italic">Which is the head of all principality and power.</hi> As the Old-Testament priesthood had its perfection in Christ, so likewise had the kingdom of David, which was the eminent principality and power under the Old Testament, and which the Jews valued themselves so much upon. And he is the Lord and head of all the powers in heaven and earth, of angels and men. <hi type="italic">Angels, and authorities, and powers are subject to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1 Pet. iii. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen32078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32079" type="x-p"/> 2. We have communion with Christ in his whole undertaking (<reference osisRef="Col.2.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Buried with him in baptism, wherein also you have risen with him.</hi> We are both buried and rise with him, and both are signified by our baptism; not that there is anything in the sign or ceremony of baptism which represents this burying and rising, any more than the crucifixion of Christ is represented by any visible resemblance in the Lord's supper: and he is speaking of the <hi type="italic">circumcision made without hands;</hi> and says it is <hi type="italic">through the faith of the operation of God.</hi> But the thing signified by our baptism is that we are buried with Christ, as baptism is the seal of the covenant and an obligation to our dying to sin; and that we are raised with Christ, as it is a seal and obligation to our living to righteousness, or newness of life. God in baptism engages to be to us a God, and we become engaged to be his people, and by his grace to die to sin and to live to righteousness, or put off the old man and put on the new.
entries.b88a647eb35cfb352f6f1e94078025d0df896281: <div eID="gen32079" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Glory of the Christian Economy. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32080" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And you, being dead in your sins and the uncircumcision of your flesh, hath he quickened together with him, having forgiven you all trespasses; <hi type="super">14</hi> Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross; <hi type="super">15</hi> <hi type="italic">And</hi> having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it. <div eID="gen32080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32081" type="x-p"/> The apostle here represents the privileges we Christians have above the Jews, which are very great. <div eID="gen32081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32082" type="x-p"/> I. Christ's death is our life: <hi type="italic">And you, being dead in your sins and the uncircumcision of your flesh, hath he quickened together with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.2.13">v. 13</reference>. A state of sin is a state of spiritual death. Those who are in sin are dead in sin. As the death of the body consists in its separation from the soul, so the death of the soul consists in its separation from God and the divine favour. As the death of the body is the corruption and putrefaction of it, so sin is the corruption or depravation of the soul. As a man who is dead is unable to help himself by any power of his own, so an habitual sinner is morally impotent: though he has a natural power, or the power of a reasonable creature, he has not a spiritual power, till he has the divine life or a renewed nature. It is principally to be understood of the Gentile world, who <hi type="italic">lay in wickedness.</hi> They were <hi type="italic">dead in the uncircumcision of their flesh,</hi> being <hi type="italic">aliens to the covenant of promise, and without God in the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.11-Eph.2.12">Eph. ii. 11, 12</reference>. By reason of their uncircumcision they were dead in their sins. It may be understood of the spiritual uncircumcision or corruption of nature; and so it shows that we are dead in law, and dead in state. Dead in law, as a condemned malefactor is called a dead man because he is under a sentence of death; so sinners by the guilt of sin are under the sentence of the law and <hi type="italic">condemned already,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.18">John iii. 18</reference>. And dead in state, by reason of the <hi type="italic">uncircumcision of our flesh.</hi> An unsanctified heart is called an <hi type="italic">uncircumcised heart:</hi> this is our state. Now through Christ we, who were dead in sins, are quickened; that is, effectual provision is made for taking away the guilt of sin, and breaking the power and dominion of it. <hi type="italic">Quickened together with him</hi>—by virtue of our union to him, and in conformity to him. Christ's death was the death of our sins; Christ's resurrection is the quickening of our souls. <div eID="gen32082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32083" type="x-p"/> II. Through him we have the remission of sin: <hi type="italic">Having forgiven you all trespasses.</hi> This is our quickening. The pardon of the crime is the life of the criminal: and this is owing to the resurrection of Christ, as well as his death; for, as he <hi type="italic">died for our sins,</hi> so he <hi type="italic">rose again for our justification,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.4.25">Rom. iv. 25</reference>. <div eID="gen32083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32084" type="x-p"/> III. Whatever was in force against us is taken out of the way. He has obtained for us a legal discharge from the <hi type="italic">hand-writing of ordinances, which was against us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.2.14">v. 14</reference>), which may be understood, 1. Of that obligation to punishment in which consists the guilt of sin. The curse of the law is the hand-writing against us, like the hand-writing on Belshazzar's wall. <hi type="italic">Cursed is every one who continues not in every thing.</hi> This was a hand-writing which was <hi type="italic">against us, and contrary to us;</hi> for it threatened our eternal ruin. This was removed when he <hi type="italic">redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.13">Gal. iii. 13</reference>. He cancelled the obligation for all who repent and believe. "Upon me be the curse, my father." He vacated and disannulled the judgment which was against us. When he was nailed to the cross, the curse was as it were nailed to the cross. And our indwelling corruption is crucified with Christ, and by virtue of his cross. When we remember the dying of the Lord Jesus, and see him nailed to the cross, we should see the hand-writing against us taken out of the way. Or rather, 2. It must be understood of the ceremonial law, the <hi type="italic">hand-writing of ordinances,</hi> the ceremonial institutions or <hi type="italic">the law of commandments contained in ordinances</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.15">Eph. ii. 15</reference>), which was a yoke to the Jews and a partition-wall to the Gentiles. The Lord Jesus <hi type="italic">took it out of the way, nailed it to his cross;</hi> that is, disannulled the obligation of it, that all might see and be satisfied that it was no more binding. When the substance came, the shadows fled away. It is abolished (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13">2 Cor. iii. 13</reference>), and <hi type="italic">that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.8.13">Heb. viii. 13</reference>. The expressions are in allusion to the ancient methods of cancelling a bond, either by crossing the writing or striking it through with a nail. <div eID="gen32084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32085" type="x-p"/> IV. He has obtained a glorious victory for us over the powers of darkness: <hi type="italic">And, having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.2.15">v. 15</reference>. As the curse of the law was against us, so the power of Satan was against us. He treated with God as the Judge, and redeemed us out of the hands of his justice by a price; but out of the hands of Satan the executioner he redeemed us by power and with a high hand. <hi type="italic">He led captivity captive.</hi> The devil and all the powers of hell were conquered and disarmed by the dying Redeemer. The first promise pointed at this; the bruising of the heel of Christ in his sufferings was the breaking of the serpent's head, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen. iii. 15</reference>. The expressions are lofty and magnificent: let us turn aside and see this great sight. The Redeemer conquered by dying. See his crown of thorns turned into a crown of laurels. He <hi type="italic">spoiled them,</hi> broke the devil's power, and conquered and disabled him, and <hi type="italic">made a show of them openly</hi>—exposed them to public shame, and made a show of them to angels and men. Never had the devil's kingdom such a mortal blow given to it as was given by the Lord Jesus. He tied them to his chariot-wheels, and rode forth conquering and to conquer—alluding to the custom of a general's triumph, who returned victorious.—<hi type="italic">Triumphing over them in it;</hi> that is, either in his cross and by his death; or, as some read it, in himself, by his own power; for he <hi type="italic">trod the wine-press alone, and of the people there was none with him.</hi>
entries.b56328bf59ee11f2bc6f2a427efa2ec21499ac1c: <div eID="gen32085" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Glory of the Christian Economy. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32086" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of a holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath <hi type="italic">days:</hi> <hi type="super">17</hi> Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body <hi type="italic">is</hi> of Christ. <hi type="super">18</hi> Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind, <hi type="super">19</hi> And not holding the Head, from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God. <hi type="super">20</hi> Wherefore if ye be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances, <hi type="super">21</hi> (Touch not; taste not; handle not; <hi type="super">22</hi> Which all are to perish with the using;) after the commandments and doctrines of men? <hi type="super">23</hi> Which things have indeed a show of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh. <div eID="gen32086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32087" type="x-p"/> The apostle concludes the chapter with exhortations to proper duty, which he infers from the foregoing discourse. <div eID="gen32087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32088" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a caution to take heed of judaizing teachers, or those who would impose upon Christians the yoke of the ceremonial law: <hi type="italic">Let no man therefore judge you in meat nor drink,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Col.2.16">v. 16</reference>. Much of the ceremonies of the law of Moses consisted in the distinction of meats and days. It appears by <reference osisRef="Rom.14.1-Rom.14.23">Rom. xiv.</reference> that there were those who were for keeping up those distinctions: but here the apostle shows that since Christ has come, and has cancelled the ceremonial law, we ought not to keep it up. "Let no man impose those things upon you, for God has not imposed them: if God has made you free, be not you again <hi type="italic">entangled in that yoke of bondage.</hi>" And this the rather because these things <hi type="italic">were shadows of things to come</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.2.17">v. 17</reference>), intimating that they had no intrinsic worth in them and that they are now done away. <hi type="italic">But the body is of Christ:</hi> the body, of which they were shadows, has come; and to continue the ceremonial observances, which were only types and shadows of Christ and the gospel, carries an intimation that Christ has not yet come and the gospel state has not yet commenced. Observe the advantages we have under the gospel, above what they had under the law: they had the shadows, we have the substance. <div eID="gen32088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32089" type="x-p"/> II. He cautions them to take heed of those who would introduce the worship of angels as mediators between God and them, as the Gentile philosophers did: <hi type="italic">Let no man beguile you of your reward, in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.2.18">v. 18</reference>. It looked like a piece of modesty to make use of the mediation of angels, as conscious to ourselves of our unworthiness to speak immediately to God; but, though it has a show of humility, it is a voluntary, not a commanded humility; and therefore it is not acceptable, yea, it is not warrantable: it is taking that honour which is due to Christ only and giving it to a creature. Besides, the notions upon which this practice was grounded were merely the inventions of men and not by divine revelation,—the proud conceits of human reason, which make a man presume to dive into things, and determine them, without sufficient knowledge and warrant: <hi type="italic">Intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind</hi>—pretending to describe the order of angels, and their respective ministries, which God has hidden from us; and therefore, though there was a show of humility in the practice, there was a real pride in the principle. They advanced those notions to gratify their own carnal fancy, and were fond of being thought wiser than other people. Pride is at the bottom of a great many errors and corruptions, and even of many evil practices, which have great show and appearance of humility. Those who do so do <hi type="italic">not hold the head,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.2.19">v. 19</reference>. They do in effect disclaim Christ, who is the only Mediator between God and man. It is the highest disparagement to Christ, who is the head of the church, for any of the members of it to make use of any intercessors with God but him. When men let go their hold of Christ, they catch at that which is next them and will stand them in no stead.—<hi type="italic">From which all the body, by joints and bands, having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God.</hi> Observe, 1. Jesus Christ is not only a head of government over the church, but a head of vital influence to it. They are knit to him by joints and bands, as the several members of the body are united to the head, and receive life and nourishment from him. 2. The body of Christ is a growing body: <hi type="italic">it increaseth with the increase of God.</hi> The new man is increasing, and the nature of grace is to grow, where there is not an accidental hindrance.—<hi type="italic">With the increase of God,</hi> with an increase of grace which is from God as its author; or, in a usual Hebraism, with a large and abundant increase.—<hi type="italic">That you may be filled with all the fulness of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.19">Eph. iii. 19</reference>. See a parallel expression, <hi type="italic">Which is the head, even Christ, from whom the whole body, fitly joined together, maketh increase of the body,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.4.15-Eph.4.16">Eph. iv. 15, 16</reference>. <div eID="gen32089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32090" type="x-p"/> III. He takes occasion hence to warn them again: "<hi type="italic">Wherefore, if you be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are you subject to ordinances?</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.2.20">v. 20</reference>. If as Christians you are dead to the observances of the ceremonial law, why are you subject to them? Such observances as, <hi type="italic">Touch not, taste not, handle not,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Col.2.21-Col.2.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. Under the law there was a ceremonial pollution contracted by touching a dead body, or any thing offered to an idol; or by tasting any forbidden meats, &c., <hi type="italic">which all are to perish with the using,</hi> having no intrinsic worth in themselves to support them, and those who used them saw them perishing and passing away; or, which tend to corrupt the Christian faith, having no other authority than the traditions and injunctions of men.—<hi type="italic">Which things have indeed a show of wisdom in will-worship and humility.</hi> They thought themselves wiser than their neighbours, in observing the law of Moses together with the gospel of Christ, that they might be sure in the one, at least, to be in the right; but, alas! it was but a show of wisdom, a mere invention and pretence. So they seem to neglect the body, by abstaining from such and such meats, and mortifying their bodily pleasures and appetites; but there is nothing of true devotion in these things, for the gospel teaches us to worship God in spirit and truth and not by ritual observances, and through the mediation of Christ alone and not of any angels. Observe, 1. Christians are freed by Christ from the ritual observances of Moses's law, and delivered from that yoke of bondage which God himself had laid upon them. 2. Subjection to ordinances, or human appointments in the worship of God, is highly blamable, and contrary to the freedom and liberty of the gospel. The apostle requires Christians <hi type="italic">to stand fast in the liberty with which Christ hath made them free, and not to be entangled again with the yoke of bondage,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.5.1">Gal. v. 1</reference>. And the imposition of them is invading the authority of Christ, the head of the church, and <hi type="italic">introducing another law of commandments contained in ordinances,</hi> when Christ has abolished the old one, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.15">Eph. ii. 15</reference>. 3. Such things have only a show of wisdom, but are really folly. It is true wisdom to keep close to the appointments of the gospel, and an entire subjection to Christ, the only head of the church.  <chapter eID="Col.2"/> <div eID="gen32090" type="x-p"/>

entries.5b4c21fbe5f52189ff80bdca6c774ad04175b149: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17854"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Col.2.1-Col.2.23">Col 2:1-23</reference>. His Strivings in Prayer for Their Steadfastness in Christ; from Whom He Warns Them Not to Be Led Away by False Wisdom.</title> <div sID="gen36340" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17854"/><hi type="bold">1. For--</hi>He explains in what respect he "labored striving" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.29">Col 1:29</reference>). Translate as Greek, "I wish you to know how great a conflict (the same Greek word as in <reference osisRef="Col.1.29">Col 1:29</reference>, "agony of a conflict" of fervent, anxious prayer; not conflict with the false teachers, which would have been impossible for him now in prison) I have for you."<div eID="gen36340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36341" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them at Laodicea--</hi>exposed to the same danger from false teachers as the Colossians (compare <reference osisRef="Col.4.16">Col 4:16</reference>). This danger was probably the cause of his writing to Laodicea, as well as to Colosse.<div eID="gen36341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36342" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not seen my face in the flesh--</hi>including those in Hierapolis (<reference osisRef="Col.4.13">Col 4:13</reference>). Paul considered himself a "debtor" to all the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.14">Ro 1:14</reference>). "His face" and presence would have been a "comfort" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.38">Ac 20:38</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Col.1.4">Col 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.8">7, 8</reference>, in proof that he had not seen, but only heard of the Colossians. Hence he strives by earnest conflict with God in anxious prayer for them, to make up for the loss of his bodily presence among them. Though "absent in the flesh, I am with you in the Spirit" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.5">Col 2:5</reference>). <div eID="gen36342" type="x-p"/>
entries.72f60a74e78b3f5d9905b349a16a522056d23618: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17855"/><div sID="gen36343" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17855"/>2. Translate, "That their hearts may be comforted." The "their," compared with "you" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.4">Col 2:4</reference>), proves that in <reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference> the words, "have not seen my face in the flesh," is a general designation of those for whom Paul declares he has "conflict," including the particular species, "you (Colossians) and them at Laodicea." For it is plain, the prayer "that their hearts may be comforted," must include in it the Colossians for whom he expressly says, "I have conflict." Thus it is an abbreviated mode of expression for, "That your and their hearts may be comforted." Alford translates, "confirmed," or allows "comforted" in its original radical sense strengthened. But the Greek supports English Version: the sense, too, is clear: comforted with the consolation of those whom Paul had not seen, and for whom, in consequence, he strove in prayerful conflict the more fervently; inasmuch as we are more anxious in behalf of absent, than present, friends [Davenant]. Their hearts would be comforted by "knowing what conflict he had for" them, and how much he is interested for their welfare; and also by being released from doubts on learning from the apostle, that the doctrine which they had heard from Epaphras was true and certain. In writing to churches which he had instructed face to face, he enters into particular details concerning them, as a father directing his children. But to those among whom he had not been in person, he treats of the more general truths of salvation.<div eID="gen36343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36344" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being--</hi>Translate as Greek in oldest manuscripts, "They being knit together."<div eID="gen36344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36345" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in love--</hi>the bond and element of perfect knitting together; the antidote to the dividing schismatical effect of false doctrine. Love to God and to one another in Christ.<div eID="gen36345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto--</hi>the object and end of their being "knit together."<div eID="gen36346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36347" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all riches--</hi>Greek, "all the riches of the full assurance (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.5">1Th 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.11">He 6:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.22">10:22</reference>) of the (Christian) understanding." The accumulation of phrases, not only "understanding," but "the full assurance of understanding"; not only this, but "the riches of," &c., not only this, but "all the riches of," &c., implies how he desires to impress them with the momentous importance of the subject in hand.<div eID="gen36347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36348" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to--</hi>Translate "unto."<div eID="gen36348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">acknowledgment--</hi>The Greek implies, "full and accurate knowledge." It is a distinct Greek word from "knowledge," <reference osisRef="Col.2.3">Col 2:3</reference>. Alford translates, "thorough ... knowledge." Acknowledgment hardly is strong enough; they did in a measure acknowledge the truth; what they wanted was the full and accurate knowledge of it (compare Notes, see on <reference osisRef="Col.1.9">Col 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.9">Php 1:9</reference>).<div eID="gen36349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36350" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of God, and of the Father and of Christ--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "and of the Father, and of"; then translate, "Of God (namely), Christ." Two very old manuscripts and Vulgate read, "Of God the Father of Christ." <div eID="gen36350" type="x-p"/>
entries.c035c45ccef63937f196f1b203db8e08bac1be96: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17856"/><div sID="gen36351" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17856"/>3. Translate in the Greek order, "In whom (not as Alford, 'in which') mystery; Christ is Himself the 'mystery' (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>), and to Christ the relative refers) are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden." The "all" here, answers to "all" in <reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>; as "treasures" answer to the "riches"; it is from the treasures that the riches (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>) are derived. "Are" is the predicate of the sentence; all the treasures ARE in Him; hidden is predicated of the state or manner in which they are in Him. Like a mine of unknown and inexhaustible wealth, the treasures of wisdom are all in Him hidden, but not in order to remain so; they only need to be explored for you to attain "unto the riches" in them (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>); but until you, Colossians, press after attaining the full knowledge (see on <reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>) of them, they remain "hidden." Compare the parable, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.44">Mt 13:44</reference>, "treasure hid." This sense suits the scope of the apostle, and sets aside Alford's objection that "the treasures are not hidden, but revealed." "Hidden" plainly answers to "mystery" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>), which is designed by God, if we be faithful to our privileges, not to remain hidden, but to be revealed (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Co 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>). Still as the mine is unfathomable, there will, through eternity, be always fresh treasures in Him to be drawn forth from their hidden state.<div eID="gen36351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wisdom--</hi>general, and as to experimental and practical truth; whence comes "understanding" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>).<div eID="gen36352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowledge--</hi>special and intellectual, in regard to doctrinal truth; whence comes "the full knowledge" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>). <div eID="gen36353" type="x-p"/>
entries.d4b01000f6533d440c01e691626ae51186af2771: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17857"/><div sID="gen36354" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17857"/><hi type="bold">4. And--</hi>"Now." Compare with "lest any man," &c. <reference osisRef="Col.2.8">Col 2:8</reference>, 16, 18. He refers to the blending of Judaism with Oriental philosophy, and the combination of this mixture with Christianity.<div eID="gen36354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36355" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enticing words--</hi>plausible as wearing the guise of wisdom and humility (<reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col 2:18</reference>, 23). <div eID="gen36355" type="x-p"/>
entries.bab0b193d161c906221446cdf804974ff49c8eb0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17858"/><div sID="gen36356" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17858"/><hi type="bold">5. For--</hi>argument against their suffering themselves to be beguiled, drawn from a regard to his personal authority as though he were present.<div eID="gen36356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36357" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">joying and beholding--</hi>beholding with joy.<div eID="gen36357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36358" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">order--</hi>your good order; answering to "knit together" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>) as a well-organized body; the same Greek as that for knit together, is used of the body" of the Church compacted," in <reference osisRef="Eph.4.16">Ep 4:16</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.33">1Co 14:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.40">40</reference>.<div eID="gen36358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">steadfastness--</hi>Greek, "the firm (or 'solid') foundation." As "order" expresses the outward aspect of the Church; so "steadfastness" expresses the inner basis on which their Church rested. The Greek literally implies not an abstract quality, but the thing in the concrete; thus their "faith" here is the solid thing which constituted the basis of their Church. <div eID="gen36359" type="x-p"/>
entries.864014db3f0ffd9389df36226a794eba8229036a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17859"/><div sID="gen36360" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17859"/>6. "As therefore ye received (once for all; the aorist tense; from Epaphras) Jesus the Christ as your Lord (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.3">1Co 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.5">2Co 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.8">Php 3:8</reference>), so walk in Him." He says not merely, "Ye received" the doctrine of Christ, but "Jesus" Himself; this is the essence of faith (<reference osisRef="John.14.21">Joh 14:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.16">Ga 1:16</reference>). Ye have received once for all the Spirit of life in Christ; carry into practice that life in your walk (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.25">Ga 5:25</reference>). This is the main scope of the Epistle. <div eID="gen36360" type="x-p"/>
entries.17690196672f401f26dd93371d1d6597aea74936: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17860"/><div sID="gen36361" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17860"/><hi type="bold">7. Rooted--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.3.17">Ep 3:17</reference>).<div eID="gen36361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36362" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">built up--</hi>Greek, "being builded up." As "rooted" implies their vitality; so "builded up," massive solidity. As in the Song of Solomon, when one image is not sufficient to express the varied aspects of divine truth, another is employed to supply the idea required. Thus "walking," a third image (<reference osisRef="Col.2.6">Col 2:6</reference>), expresses the thought which "rooted" and "built," though each suggesting a thought peculiar to itself, could not express, namely, onward motion. "Rooted" is in the past tense, implying their first conversion and vital grafting "in Him." "Built up" is present (in the Greek), implying their progressive increase in religion by union with Him. <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Ep 2:20</reference> refers to the Church; but the passage here to their individual progress in edification (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.32">Ac 20:32</reference>).<div eID="gen36362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stablished--</hi>confirmed.<div eID="gen36363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as--</hi>"even as."<div eID="gen36364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36365" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abounding therein with thanksgiving--</hi>advancing to fuller maturity (compare <reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>) in the faith, "with thanksgiving" to God as the gracious Author of this whole blessing. <div eID="gen36365" type="x-p"/>
entries.9155444cacb1ddd266a973756e4a13c78acb01c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17861"/><div sID="gen36366" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17861"/>8. Translate, "Beware (literally, 'Look' well) lest there shall be (as I fear there is: the Greek indicative expresses this) any man (pointing to some known emissary of evil, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.7">Ga 1:7</reference>) leading you away as his spoil (not merely gaining spoil out of you, but making yourselves his spoil) through (by means of) his philosophy," &c. The apostle does not condemn all philosophy, but "the philosophy" (so Greek) of the Judaic-oriental heretics at Colosse, which afterwards was developed into Gnosticism. You, who may have "the riches of full assurance" and "the treasures of wisdom," should not suffer yourselves to be led away as a spoil by empty, deceitful philosophy: "riches" are contrasted with spoil; "full" with "vain," or empty (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.9">3, 9</reference>).<div eID="gen36366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after--</hi>"according to."<div eID="gen36367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tradition of men--</hi>opposed to, "the fulness of the Godhead." Applied to Rabbinical traditions, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.8">Mr 7:8</reference>. When men could not make revelation even seem to tell about deep mysteries which they were curious to pry into, they brought in human philosophy and pretended traditions to help it, as if one should bring a lamp to the sundial to find the hour [Cauations for Times, p. 85]. The false teachers boasted of a higher wisdom in theory, transmitted by tradition among the initiated; in practice they enjoined asceticism, as though matter and the body were the sources of evil. Phrygia (in which was Colosse) had a propensity for the mystical and magical, which appeared in their worship of Cybele and subsequent Montanism [Neander].<div eID="gen36368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rudiments of the world--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Gal.4.3">Ga 4:3</reference>). "The rudiments" or elementary lessons "of the (outward) world," such as legal ordinances; our Judaic childhood's lessons (<reference osisRef="Col.2.11">Col 2:11</reference>, 16, 20; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.1-Gal.4.3">Ga 4:1-3</reference>). But Neander, "the elements of the world," in the sense, what is earthly, carnal and outward, not "the rudiments of religion," in Judaism and heathenism.<div eID="gen36369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36370" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not after Christ--</hi>"Their" boasted higher "philosophy" is but human tradition, and a cleaving to the carnal and worldly, and not to Christ. Though acknowledging Christ nominally, in spirit they by their doctrine deny Him. <div eID="gen36370" type="x-p"/>
entries.de6e67650215f05bd834f15736312b5a5494f9cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17862"/><div sID="gen36371" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17862"/><hi type="bold">9. For--</hi>"Because." Their "philosophy" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.8">Col 2:8</reference>) is not "after Christ," as all true philosophy is, everything which comes not from, and tends not to, Him, being a delusion; "For in Him (alone) dwelleth" as in a temple, &c.<div eID="gen36371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the fulness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Col.1.19">Col 1:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.10">Joh 14:10</reference>).<div eID="gen36372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36373" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the Godhead--</hi>The Greek (theotes) means the ESSENCE and NATURE of the Godhead, not merely the divine perfections and attributes of Divinity (Greek, "theiotes"). He, as man, was not merely God-like, but in the fullest sense, God.<div eID="gen36373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36374" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bodily--</hi>not merely as before His incarnation, but now "bodily in Him" as the incarnate word (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference>). Believers, by union with Him, partake of His fulness of the divine nature (<reference osisRef="John.1.16">Joh 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.4">2Pe 1:4</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Eph.3.19">Ep 3:19</reference>). <div eID="gen36374" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1093a159c70ea2aa9454fdf25c5cdb14422740f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17863"/><div sID="gen36375" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17863"/><hi type="bold">10. And--</hi>And therefore; and so. Translate in the Greek order, "Ye are in Him (by virtue of union with Him) filled full" of all that you need (<reference osisRef="John.1.16">Joh 1:16</reference>). Believers receive of the divine unction which flows down from their Divine Head and High Priest (<reference osisRef="Ps.133.2">Psa 133:2</reference>). He is full of the "fulness" itself; we, filled from Him. Paul implies, Therefore ye Colossians need no supplementary sources of grace, such as the false teachers dream of. Christ is "the Head of all rule and authority" (so the Greek), <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference>; He, therefore, alone, not these subject "authorities" also, is to be adored (<reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col 2:18</reference>). <div eID="gen36375" type="x-p"/>
entries.91807adb43dc8e135831f9904ec0984531f8f510: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17864"/><div sID="gen36376" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17864"/>11. Implying that they did not need, as the Judaizers taught, the outward rite of circumcision, since they had already the inward spiritual reality of it.<div eID="gen36376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are--</hi>rather, as the Greek, "Ye were (once for all) circumcised (spiritually, at your conversion and baptism, <reference osisRef="Rom.2.28">Ro 2:28</reference>, 29; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.3">Php 3:3</reference>) with a (so the Greek) circumcision made without hands"; opposed to "the circumcision in the flesh made by hands" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.11">Ep 2:11</reference>). Christ's own body, by which the believer is sanctified, is said to be "not made with hands" (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.58">Mr 14:58</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.11">He 9:11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Dan.2.45">Da 2:45</reference>).<div eID="gen36377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36378" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in putting off--</hi>rather as Greek, "in your putting off"; as an old garment (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.22">Ep 4:22</reference>); alluding to the putting off the foreskin in circumcision.<div eID="gen36378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36379" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the body of the sins of the flesh--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "the body of the flesh," omitting "of the sins," that is, "the body," of which the prominent feature is fleshiness (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.8.13">Ro 8:13</reference>, where "flesh" and "the body" mutually correspond). This fleshly body, in its sinful aspect, is put off in baptism (where baptism answers its ideal) as the seal of regeneration where received in repentance and faith. In circumcision the foreskin only was put off; in Christian regeneration "the body of the flesh" is spiritually put off, at least it is so in its ideal conception, however imperfectly believers realize that ideal.<div eID="gen36379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36380" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by--</hi>Greek, "in." This spiritual circumcision is realized in, or by, union with Christ, whose "circumcision," whereby He became responsible for us to keep the whole law, is imputed to believers for justification; and union with whom, in all His vicarious obedience, including His circumcision, is the source of our sanctification. Alford makes it explanatory of the previous, "a circumcision made without hands," namely, "the circumcision brought about by your union with Christ." The former view seems to me better to accord with <reference osisRef="Col.2.12">Col 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.4">3, 4</reference>, which similarly makes the believer, by spiritual union with Christ, to have personal fellowship in the several states of Christ, namely, His death, resurrection, and appearing in glory. Nothing was done or suffered by our Mediator as such, but may be acted in our souls and represented in our spirits. Pearson's view, however, is that of Alford. Joshua, the type (not Moses in the wilderness), circumcised the Israelites in Canaan (<reference osisRef="Josh.5.2-Josh.5.9">Jos 5:2-9</reference>) the second time: the people that came out of Egypt having been circumcised, and afterwards having died in the wilderness; but those born after the Exodus not having been so. Jesus, the Antitype, is the author of the true circumcision, which is therefore called "the circumcision of Christ" (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Ro 2:29</reference>). As Joshua was "Moses' minister," so Jesus, "minister of the circumcision for the truth of God" unto the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.8">Ro 15:8</reference>). <div eID="gen36380" type="x-p"/>
entries.18ce33c6818daed14ed29e52bc02e0e19bc2d21a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17865"/><div sID="gen36381" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17865"/>12. Translate, "Having been buried with Him in your baptism." The past participle is here coincident in time with the preceding verb, "ye were (Greek) circumcised." Baptism is regarded as the burial of the old carnal life, to which the act of immersion symbolically corresponds; and in warm climates where immersion is safe, it is the mode most accordant with the significance of the ordinance; but the spirit of the ordinance is kept by affusion, where immersion would be inconvenient or dangerous; to insist on literal immersion in all cases would be mere legal ceremonialism (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.3">Ro 6:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen36381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36382" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are risen--</hi>rather as Greek, "were raised with Him."<div eID="gen36382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36383" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through the faith, &c.--</hi>by means of your faith in the operation of God; so "faith of," for "faith in" (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.12">Ep 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.9">Php 3:9</reference>). Faith in God's mighty operation in raising again Jesus, is saving faith (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.24">Ro 4:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.9">10:9</reference>); and it is wrought in the soul by His same "mighty working" whereby He "raised Jesus from the dead" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>). Bengel seems to me (not as Alford understands him) to express the latter sense, namely, "Through the faith which is a work of the operation of God who," &c. <reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference> accords with this; the same mighty power of God is exercised in raising one spiritually dead to the life of faith, as was "wrought in Christ when God raised Him literally from the dead." However, "faith of" usually is "faith in" (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.22">Ro 3:22</reference>); but there is no grammatical impropriety in understanding it "the faith which is the effect of the operation of God" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.8">Ep 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.13">1Th 2:13</reference>). As His literal resurrection is the ground of the power put forth in our spiritual resurrection now, so it is a pledge of our literal resurrection hereafter (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.11">Ro 8:11</reference>). <div eID="gen36383" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b6ff11816691176704ee87e69a82d2fcef04eea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17866"/><div sID="gen36384" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17866"/><hi type="bold">13. you, being dead--</hi>formerly (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.1">Ep 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>); even as Christ was among the dead, before that God raised Him "from the dead" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.12">Col 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen36384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36385" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sins--</hi>rather as Greek is translated at end of this verse, "trespasses," literally, "failings aside" from God's ways; actual transgressions, as that of Adam.<div eID="gen36385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36386" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">uncircumcision of your flesh--</hi>your not having put off the old fleshly nature, the carnal foreskin, or original sin, which now by spiritual circumcision, that is, conversion and baptism, you have put off.<div eID="gen36386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36387" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he quickened--</hi>God "quickened together with Him (Christ)." Just as Christ's resurrection proved that He was delivered from the sin laid on Him, so our spiritual quickening proves that we have been forgiven our sins (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1Pe 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.1">4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2</reference>).<div eID="gen36387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forgiven you--</hi>So Vulgate and Hilary. But the oldest manuscripts read, "us," passing from the particular persons, the Colossians, to the general Church (<reference osisRef="Col.1.14">Col 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>).<div eID="gen36388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all trespasses--</hi>Greek, "all our trespasses." <div eID="gen36389" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c592d5fd48e34ed556f5aba3e99574e16f739e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17867"/><div sID="gen36390" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17867"/><hi type="bold">14. Blotting out--</hi>Greek, "Having wiped out"; coincident in time with "having forgiven you" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.13">Col 2:13</reference>); hereby having cancelled the law's indictment against you. The law (including especially the moral law, wherein lay the chief difficulty in obeying) is abrogated to the believer, as far as it was a compulsory, accusing code, and as far as "righteousness" (justification) and "life" were sought for by it. It can only produce outward works, not inward obedience of the will, which in the believer flows from the Holy Spirit in Him (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.21">Ro 3:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.7.2">7:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.19">Ga 2:19</reference>).<div eID="gen36390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36391" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the handwriting of ordinances--</hi>rather, "IN ordinances" (see on <reference osisRef="Eph.2.15">Ep 2:15</reference>); "the law of commandments contained in ordinances." "The handwriting" (alluding to the Decalogue, the representative of the law, written by the hand of God) is the whole law, the obligatory bond, under which all lay; the Jews primarily were under the bond, but they in this respect were the representative people of the world (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.19">Ro 3:19</reference>); and in their inability to keep the law was involved the inability of the Gentiles also, in whose hearts "the work of the law was written" (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.15">Ro 2:15</reference>); and as they did not keep this, they were condemned by it.<div eID="gen36391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36392" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that was against us ... contrary to us--</hi>Greek "adversary to us"; so it is translated, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.27">He 10:27</reference>. "Not only was the law against us by its demands, but also an adversary to us by its accusations" [Bengel]. Tittmann explains the Greek, "having a latent contrariety to us"; not open designed hostility, but virtual unintentional opposition through our frailty; not through any opposition in the law itself to our good (Ro 7:7-12, 14; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.56">1Co 15:56</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.21">Ga 3:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.3">He 10:3</reference>). The "WRITING" is part of "that which was contrary to us"; for "the letter killeth" (see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">2Co 3:6</reference>).<div eID="gen36392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36393" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and took it--</hi>Greek, and hath taken it out of the way" (so as to be no longer a hindrance to us), by "nailing it to the cross." Christ, by bearing the curse of the broken law, has redeemed us from its curse (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.13">Ga 3:13</reference>). In His person nailed to the cross, the law itself was nailed to it. One ancient mode of cancelling bonds was by striking a nail through the writing: this seems at that time to have existed in Asia [Grotius]. The bond cancelled in the present case was the obligation lying against the Jews as representatives of the world, and attested by their amen, to keep the whole law under penalty of the curse (<reference osisRef="Deut.27.26">De 27:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.10.29">Ne 10:29</reference>). <div eID="gen36393" type="x-p"/>
entries.924a5659d92e60cc2570e3ecfac76ca070f560a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17868"/><div sID="gen36394" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17868"/>15. Alford, Ellicott, and others translate the Greek to accord with the translation of the same Greek, <reference osisRef="Col.3.9">Col 3:9</reference>, "Stripping off from Himself the principalities and the powers: " God put off from Himself the angels, that is, their ministry, not employing them to be promulgators of the Gospel in the way that He had given the law by their "disposition" or ministry (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.53">Ac 7:53</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.19">Ga 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.2">He 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5">5</reference>): God manifested Himself without a veil in Jesus. "The principalities and THE powers" refers back to <reference osisRef="Col.2.10">Col 2:10</reference>, Jesus, "the Head of all principality and power," and <reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col 1:16</reference>. In the sacrifice of Jesus on the cross, God subjected all the principalities, &c., to Jesus, declaring them to be powerless as to His work and His people (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.21">Ep 1:21</reference>). Thus Paul's argument against those grafting on Christianity Jewish observances, along with angel-worship, is, whatever part angels may be supposed to have had under the law, now at an end, God having put the legal dispensation itself away. But the objection is, that the context seems to refer to a triumph over bad angels: in <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">2Co 2:14</reference>, however, Christ's triumph over those subjected to Him, is not a triumph for destruction, but for their salvation, so that good angels may be referred to (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>). But the Greek middle is susceptible of English Version, "having spoiled," or, literally [Tittmann], "having completely stripped," or "despoiled" for Himself (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.8.38">Ro 8:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1Co 15:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.2">Ep 6:2</reference>). English Version accords with <reference osisRef="Matt.12.29">Mt 12:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.11.22">Lu 11:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>. Translate as the Greek, "The rules and authorities."<div eID="gen36394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36395" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made a show of them--</hi>at His ascension (see on <reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Ep 4:8</reference>; confirming English Version of this verse).<div eID="gen36395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36396" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">openly--</hi><reference osisRef="John.7.4">Joh 7:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.11.54">11:54</reference>, support English Version against Alford's translation, "in openness of speech."<div eID="gen36396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36397" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in it--</hi>namely, His cross, or crucifixion: so the Greek fathers translate. Many of the Latins, "In Himself" or "in Him." <reference osisRef="Eph.2.16">Ep 2:16</reference> favors English Version, "reconcile ... by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby." If "in Him," that is, Christ, be read, still the Cross will be the place and means of God's triumph in Christ over the principalities (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.20">Ep 1:20</reference>; 2:5). Demons, like other angels, were in heaven up to Christ's ascension, and influenced earth from their heavenly abodes. As heaven was not yet opened to man before Christ (<reference osisRef="John.3.13">Joh 3:13</reference>), so it was not yet shut against demons (<reference osisRef="Job.1.6">Job 1:6</reference>; 2:1). But at the ascension Satan and his demons were "judged" and "cast out" by Christ's obedience unto death (<reference osisRef="John.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.11">16:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.5-Rev.12.10">Re 12:5-10</reference>), and the Son of man was raised to the throne of God; thus His resurrection and ascension are a public solemn triumph over the principalities and powers of death. It is striking that the heathen oracles were silenced soon after Christ's ascension. <div eID="gen36397" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d178028c1776b644259247757ab4950effae817: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17869"/><div sID="gen36398" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17869"/><hi type="bold">16. therefore--</hi>because ye are complete in Christ, and God in Him has dispensed with all subordinate means as essential to acceptance with Him.<div eID="gen36398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36399" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">meat ... drink--</hi>Greek, "eating ... drinking" (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.1-Rom.14.17">Ro 14:1-17</reference>). Pay no regard to any one who sits in judgment on you as to legal observances in respect to foods.<div eID="gen36399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36400" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holyday--</hi>a feast yearly. Compare the three, <reference osisRef="1Chr.23.31">1Ch 23:31</reference>.<div eID="gen36400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36401" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">new moon--</hi>monthly.<div eID="gen36401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sabbath--</hi>Omit "THE," which is not in the Greek (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Gal.4.10">Ga 4:10</reference>). "Sabbaths" (not "the sabbaths") of the day of atonement and feast of tabernacles have come to an end with the Jewish services to which they belonged (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.32">Le 23:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.37-Lev.23.39">37-39</reference>). The weekly sabbath rests on a more permanent foundation, having been instituted in Paradise to commemorate the completion of creation in six days. <reference osisRef="Lev.23.38">Le 23:38</reference> expressly distinguished "the sabbath of the Lord" from the other sabbaths. A positive precept is right because it is commanded, and ceases to be obligatory when abrogated; a moral precept is commanded eternally, because it is eternally right. If we could keep a perpetual sabbath, as we shall hereafter, the positive precept of the sabbath, one in each week, would not be needed. <reference osisRef="Heb.4.9">He 4:9</reference>, "rests," Greek, "keeping of sabbath" (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.23">Is 66:23</reference>). But we cannot, since even Adam, in innocence, needed one amidst his earthly employments; therefore the sabbath is still needed and is therefore still linked with the other nine commandments, as obligatory in the spirit, though the letter of the law has been superseded by that higher spirit of love which is the essence of law and Gospel alike (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.8-Rom.13.10">Ro 13:8-10</reference>). <div eID="gen36402" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1554e06f110b88156ae567a72ef0372043fcbb1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17870"/><div sID="gen36403" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17870"/><hi type="bold">17. things to come--</hi>the blessings of the Christian covenant, the substance of which Jewish ordinances were but the type. Compare "ages to come," that is, the Gospel dispensation (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.7">Ep 2:7</reference>). <reference osisRef="Heb.2.5">He 2:5</reference>, "the world to come."<div eID="gen36403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the body is of Christ--</hi>The real substance (of the blessings typified by the law) belongs to Christ (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.5">He 8:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.1">10:1</reference>). <div eID="gen36404" type="x-p"/>
entries.4cf38241358658888092e7211371cb73a979c4c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17871"/><div sID="gen36405" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17871"/><hi type="bold">18. beguile--</hi>Translate, "Defraud you of your prize," literally, "to adjudge a prize out of hostility away from him who deserves it" [Trench]. "To be umpire in a contest to the detriment of one." This defrauding of their prize the Colossians would suffer, by letting any self-constituted arbitrator or judge (that is, false teacher) draw them away from Christ," the righteous Judge" and Awarder of the prize (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.12">Jas 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.4">1Pe 5:4</reference>), to angel-worship.<div eID="gen36405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36406" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in a voluntary humility--</hi>So "will-worship" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.23">Col 2:23</reference>). Literally, "Delighting ([Wahl]) in humility"; loving (so the Greek is translated, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.38">Mr 12:38</reference>, "love to go in long clothing") to indulge himself in a humility of his own imposing: a volunteer in humility [Dallæus]. Not as Alford, "Let no one of purpose defraud you," &c. Not as Grotius, "If he ever so much wish" (to defraud you). For the participle "wishing" or "delighting," is one of the series, and stands in the same category as "intruding," "puffed up," "not holding"; and the self-pleasing implied in it stands in happy contrast to the (mock) humility with which it seems to me, therefore, to be connected. His "humility," so called, is a pleasing of self: thus it stands in parallelism to "his fleshly mind" (its real name, though he styles it "humility"), as "wishing" or "delighting" does to "puffed up." The Greek for "humility" is literally, "lowliness of mind," which forms a clearer parallel to "puffed up by his fleshly mind." Under pretext of humility, as if they durst not come directly to God and Christ (like the modern Church of Rome), they invoked angels: as Judaizers, they justified this on the ground that the law was given by angels. This error continued long in Phrygia (where Colosse and Laodicea were), so that the Council of Laodicea (A.D. 360) expressly framed its thirty-fifth canon against the "Angelici" (as Augustine [Heresies, 39], calls them) or "invokers of angels." Even as late as Theodoret's time, there were oratories to Michael the archangel. The modern Greeks have a legend that Michael opened a chasm to draw off an inundation threatening the Colossian Christians. Once men admit the inferior powers to share invocation with the Supreme, the former gradually engrosses all our serious worship, almost to the exclusion of the latter; thus the heathen, beginning with adding the worship of other deities to that of the Supreme, ended with ceasing to worship Him at all. Nor does it signify much, whether we regard such as directly controlling us (the pagan view), or as only influencing the Supreme in our behalf (the Church of Rome's view); because he from whom I expect happiness or misery, becomes the uppermost object in my mind, whether he give, or only procure it [Cautions for Times]. Scripture opposes the idea of "patrons" or "intercessors" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5">1Ti 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.6">6</reference>).
