Those, therefore, who still adhere to those <hi type="italic">shadows</hi>, act like one who should judge of a man’s appearance from his shadow, while in the mean time he had himself personally before his eyes. For Christ is now manifested to us, and hence we enjoy him as being present. <hi type="italic">The body</hi>, says he, <hi type="italic">is of Christ</hi>, that is, IN <hi type="italic">Christ</hi>. For the substance of those things which the ceremonies anciently prefigured is now presented before our eyes in Christ, inasmuch as he contains in himself everything that they marked out as future. Hence, the man that calls back the ceremonies into use, either buries the manifestation of Christ, or robs Christ of his excellence, and makes him in a manner void. <note n="387"> <div sID="gen127483" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Inutile et du tout vuide</foreign>;” — “Useless and altogether void.”<div eID="gen127483" type="x-p"/> </note> Accordingly, should any one of mortals assume to himself in this matter the office of judge, let us not submit to him, inasmuch as Christ, the only competent Judge, sets us free. For when he says, <hi type="italic">Let no man judge you</hi>, he does not address the false apostles, but prohibits the Colossians from yielding their neck to unreasonable requirements. To abstain, it is true, from swine’s flesh, is in itself harmless, but the binding to do it is pernicious, because it makes void the grace of Christ.<div eID="gen127482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen127484" type="x-p"/>Should any one ask, “What view, then, is to be taken of our sacraments? Do they not also represent Christ to us as absent?” I answer, that they differ widely from the ancient ceremonies. For as painters do not in the first draught bring out a likeness in vivid colors, and (<foreign xml:lang="el">εἰκονικῶς</foreign>) <hi type="italic">expressively</hi>, but in the first instance draw rude and obscure lines with charcoal, so the representation of Christ under the law was unpolished, and was, as it were, a first sketch, but in our sacraments it is seen drawn out to the life. Paul, however, had something farther in view, for he contrasts the bare aspect of the <hi type="italic">shadow</hi> with the solidity of the <hi type="italic">body</hi>, and admonishes them, that it is the part of a madman to take hold of empty shadows, when it is in his power to handle the solid substance. Farther, while our sacraments represent Christ as absent as to view and distance of place, it is in such a manner as to testify that he has been once manifested, and they now also present him to us to be enjoyed. They are not, therefore, bare shadows, but on the contrary symbols <note n="388"> <div sID="gen127485" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Signes et tesmoignages</foreign>;” — “Signs and evidences.”<div eID="gen127485" type="x-p"/> </note> of Christ’s presence, for they contain that <hi type="italic">Yea</hi> <hi type="italic">and</hi> <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> of all the <hi type="italic">promises</hi> <hi type="italic">of</hi> <hi type="italic">God</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.1.20">2 Corinthians 1:20</reference>,) which has been once manifested to us in Christ.<div eID="gen127484" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Col.2.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen127481" osisID="Col.2.17" type="section"/>
entries.871e68682c4aa51a69bf6d8e717b82178c684adb:
18. Let no one take from you the palm.
“The Latin, ‘seducat,’ correctly gives the intention of καταβραβευέτω which signifies, to cause a competitor to lose his prize, by drawing him aside from the goal, (seorsim ducendo, or seducendo.)” — Penn. — Ed.
He alludes to runners, or wrestlers, to whom the palm was assigned, on condition of their not giving way in the middle of the course, or after the contest had been commenced. He admonishes them, therefore, that the false apostles aimed at nothing else than to snatch away from them the palm, inasmuch as they draw them aside from the rectitude of their course. Hence it follows that they must be shunned as the most injurious pests. The passage is also carefully to be marked as intimating, that all those who draw us aside from the simplicity of Christ cheat us out of the prize of our high calling. (Philippians 3:14.)
Desirous in humility. Something must be understood; hence I have, inserted in the text id facere, (to do it.) For he points out the kind of danger which they required to guard against. All are desirous to defraud you of the palm, who, under the pretext of humility, recommend to you the worship of angels. For their object is, that you may wander out of the way, leaving the one object of aim. I read humility and worship of angels conjointly, for the one follows the other, just as at this day the Papists make use of the same pretext when philosophizing as to the worship of saints. For they reason on the ground of man’s abasement,
“Car ayans proposé l’indignite de l’homme, et presché d’humilite, de là ils concluent;” — “For having set forth man’s unworthiness, and having preached of humility, they conclude from this.”
that we must, therefore, seek for mediators to help us. But for this very reason has Christ humbled himself — that we might directly betake ourselves to him, however miserable sinners we may be.
I am aware that the worship of angels is by many interpreted otherwise, as meaning such as has been delivered to men by angels; for the Devil has always endeavored to set off his impostures under this title. The Pope at this day boasts, that all the trifles with which he has adulterated the pure worship of God are revelations. In like manner the Theurgians
The Theurgians were the followers of Ammonius Saccas, who prescribed an austere discipline with the view of “refining,” as he pretended, “that faculty of the mind which receives the images of things, so as to render it capable of perceiving the demons, and of performing many marvellous things by their assistance.” See Mosheim’s, Ecclesiastical History, vol. 1, p. 174. — Ed.
of old alleged that all the superstitions that they contrived were delivered over to them by angels, as if from hand to hand.
Per manus, (from one hand to another.) The reader will find the same proverbial expression made use of by Calvin on the Corinthians, vol. 1, pp. 150, 373, and vol. 2, p. 9. — Ed.
They, accordingly, think that Paul here condemns all fanciful kinds of worship that are falsely set forth under the authority of angels.
“Lesquelles on fait receuoir au poure monde sous la fausse couuerture de l’authorite des anges;” — “Which they make the world receive under the false pretext of the authority of angels.”
But, in my opinion, he rather condemns the contrivance as to the worshipping of angels. It is on this account that he has so carefully applied himself to this in the very commencement of the Epistle, to bring angels under subjection, lest they should obscure the splendor of Christ.
“La splendeur de la maieste de Christ;” — “The splendor of Christ’s majesty.”
In fine, as he had in the first chapter prepared the way for abolishing the ceremonies, so he had also for the removal of all other hinderances which draw us away from Christ alone.
“De seul vray but, qui est Christ;” — “From the only true aim, which is Christ.”
In this class is the worship of angels
Superstitious persons have from the beginning worshipped angels,
See Calvin’S Institutes, vol. 1, p. 200.
that through means of them there might be free access to God. The Platonists infected the Christian Church also with this error. For although Augustine sharply inveighs against them in his tenth book “On the City of God,” and condemns at great length all their disputations as to the worship of angels, we see nevertheless what has happened. Should any one compare the writings of Plato with Popish theology, he will find that they have drawn wholly from Plato their prattling as to the worship of angels. The sum is this, that we must honor angels, whom Plato calls demons, χάριν τὢς εὐφήμου διαπορείας (for the sake of their auspicious intercession.)
“A cause de l’heureuse intercession qu’ils font pour les hommes;” — “On account of the blessed intercession which they make for men.”
He brings forward this sentiment in Epinomis, and he confirms it in Cratylus,
See Calvin’S Institutes, vol. 1, p. 202.
and many other passages. In what respect do the Papists differ at all from this? “But,” it will be said, “they do not deny that the Son of God is Mediator.” Neither did those with whom Paul contends; but as they imagined that God must be approached by the assistance of the angels, and that, consequently, some worship must be rendered to them, so they placed angels in the seat of Christ, and honored them with Christ’s office. Let us know, then, that Paul here condemns all kinds of worship of human contrivance, which are rendered either to angels or to the dead, as though they were mediators, rendering assistance after Christ, or along with Christ.
“Comme s’ils estoyent mediateurs ou auec Christ, ou en second lieu apres Christ, pour suppleer ce qui defaut de son costé“ — “As if they were mediators either with Christ, or in the second place after Christ, to supply what is wanting on his part.”
For just so far do we recede from Christ, when we transfer the smallest part of what belongs to him to any others, whether they be angels or men.
Intruding into those things which he hath not seen. The verb ἐμβατεύειν, the participle of which Paul here makes use of, has various significations. The rendering which Erasmus, after Jerome, has given to it, walking proudly, would not suit ill, were there an example of such a signification in any author of sufficient note. For we see every day with how much confidence and pride rash persons pronounce an opinion as to things unknown. Nay, even in the very subject of which Paul treats, there is a remarkable illustration. For when the Sorbonnic divines put forth their trifles
“Mettent en auant leurs mensonges;” — “Bring forward their false hoods.”
respecting the intercession of saints or angels, they declare,
“Ils prononcent et determinent comme par arrest;” — “They declare and determine as if by decree.”
as though it were from an oracle,
“Perinde atque ex tripode,” (just as though it were from the tripod.) Our author manifestly alludes to the three-footed stool on which the Priestess of Apollo at Delphi sat, while giving forth oracular responses. — Ed.
that the dead
“Les saincts trespassez;” — “Departed saints.”
know and behold our necessities, inasmuch as they see all things in the reflex light of God.
“En la reuerberation de la lumiere de Dieu;” — “In the reflection of the light of God.”
And yet, what is less certain? Nay more, what is more obscure and doubtful? But such, truly, is their magisterial freedom, that they fearlessly and daringly assert what is not only not known by them, but cannot be known by men.
This meaning, therefore, would be suitable, if that signification of the term were usual. It is, however, among the Greeks taken simply as meaning to walk. It also sometimes means to inquire. Should any one choose to understand it thus in this passage, Paul will, in that case, reprove a foolish curiosity in the investigation of things that are obscure, and such as are even hid from our view and transcend it.
“Et surmontent toute nostre capacite;” — “And exceed all our capacity.”
It appears to me, however, that I have caught Paul’s meaning, and have rendered it faithfully in this manner — intruding into those things which he hath not seen. For that is the common signification of the word ἐμβατεύειν — to enter upon an inheritance,
Thus ἐμβατεύειν εἰς τὴν οὐσίαν is made use of by Demosthenes, as meaning — “to come in to the property.” — See Dem. 1086. 19. — Ed.
or to take possession, or to set foot anywhere. Accordingly, Budaeus renders this passage thus: — “Setting foot upon, or entering on the possession of those things which he has not seen.” I have followed his authority, but have selected a more suitable term. For such persons in reality break through and intrude into secret things,
“Es choses secretes et cachees;” — “Into things secret and hidden.”
of which God would have no discovery as yet made to us. The passage ought to be carefully observed, for the purpose of reproving the rashness
“La role outrecuidance;” — “The foolish presumption.”
of those who inquire farther than is allowable.
Puffed up in vain by a fleshly mind. He employs the expression fleshly mind to denote the perspicuity of the human intellect, however great it may be. For he places it in contrast with that spiritual wisdom which is revealed to us from heaven in accordance with that statement —
Flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee. (Matthew 16:17.)
Whoever; therefore, depends upon his own reason, inasmuch as the acuteness of the flesh is wholly at work in him,
“Pource qu’il n’est gouuerné que par la subtilite charnelle et naturelle;” — “Because he is regulated exclusively by carnal and natural acuteness.”
Paul declares him to be puffed up in vain. And truly all the wisdom that men have from themselves is mere wind: hence there is nothing solid except in the word of God and the illumination of the Spirit. And observe, that those are said to be puffed up who insinuate themselves
“En la grace des hommes;” — “Into the favor of men.
under a show of humility. For it happens, as Augustine elegantly writes to Paulinus, by wonderful means, as to the soul of man, that it is more puffed up from a false humility than if it were openly proud.
entries.5b8b7db008a26b5cd9edea242d539bd8c429ffeb:
19. Not holding the Head. He condemns in the use of one word whatever does not bear a relation to Christ. He also confirms his statement on the ground that all things flow from him, and depend upon him. Hence, should any one call us anywhere else than to Christ, though in other respects he were big with heaven and earth, he is empty and full of wind: let us, therefore, without concern, bid him farewell. Observe, however, of whom he is speaking, namely, of those who did not openly reject or deny Christ, but, not accurately understanding his office and power, by seeking out other helps and means of salvation, (as they commonly speak,) were not firmly rooted in him.
From whom the whole body by joints. He simply means this, that the Church does not stand otherwise than in the event of all things being furnished to her by Christ, the Head, and, accordingly, that her entire safety
“Toute la perfection de son estre;” — “The entire perfection of her being.”
consists in him. The body, it is true, has its nerves, its joints, and ligaments, but all these things derive their vigor solely from the Head, so that the whole binding of them together is from that source. What, then, must be done? The constitution of the body will be in a right state, if simply the Head, which furnishes the several members with everything that they have, is allowed, without any hinderance, to have the pre-eminence. This Paul speaks of as the increase of God, by which he means that it is not every increase that is approved by God, but only that which has a relation to the Head. For we see that the kingdom of the Pope is not merely tall and large, but swells out into a monstrous size. As, however, we do not there see what Paul here requires in the Church, what shall we say, but that it is a humpbacked body, and a confused mass that will fall to pieces of itself.
Colossians 2:20-23
20. Wherefore if ye be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances,
20. Si igitur mortui estis cum Christo ab elementis huius mundi, quid tanquam viventibus in mundo decreta vobis perscribuntur?
21. (Touch not; taste not; handle not;
21. Ne esitaveris, ne gustaveris, ne attigeris:
22. Which all are to perish with the using;) after the commandments and doctrines of men?
22. Quae sunt omnia in corruptionem ipso abusu, secundum praecepta et doctrines hominum,
23. Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
23. Quae speciem
“Espece, ou, forme;” — “Appearance, or form.”
quidem habent sapientiae in superstitione,
“Superstition, or will-worship.”
et humilitate animi, et neglectu corporis:
“En mespris du corps, ou, en ce qu’elles n’espargnent le corps;” — “In contempt of the body, or, inasmuch as they do not spare the body.”
non in honore aliquo ad expletionem carnis.
“Sans aucun honneur a rassasier la chair, ou, et ne ont aucun esgard au rassasiement d’iceluy: ou, mais ne font d’aucune estime, n’appartenans qu’a ce qui remplit le corps;” — “Without any honour to the satisfying of the flesh, or, and they have no regard to the satisfying of it, or, but they hold it in no esteem, not caring as to what fills the body.”
entries.ded2be7214d553865a0b619a45d4784b1ae13635: <div annotateRef="Bible:Col.2.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Col.2.20" sID="gen127537" type="section"/> <div sID="gen127538" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20. </hi><hi type="italic">If ye are dead</hi>. He had previously said, that the ordinances were fastened to the cross of Christ. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Col.2.14">Colossians 2:14</reference>.) He now employs another figure of speech — that we are <hi type="italic">dead</hi> to them, as he teaches us elsewhere, that we are <hi type="italic">dead</hi> <hi type="italic">to</hi> <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">law</hi>, and the law, on the other hand, to us. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.2.19">Galatians 2:19</reference>.) The term death means abrogation, <note n="416"> <div sID="gen127539" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et abolissement</foreign>;” — “And abolishment.”<div eID="gen127539" type="x-p"/> </note> but it is more expressive <hi type="italic">and</hi> <hi type="italic">more</hi> <hi type="italic">emphatic</hi>, (<foreign xml:lang="el">καὶ ἐμφατικώτερον</foreign>.) He says, therefore, that the Colossians, have nothing to do with ordinances. Why? Because they have died with Christ to ordinances; that is, after they died with Christ by regeneration, they were, through his kindness, set free from ordinances, that they may not belong to them any more. Hence he concludes that they are by no means bound by the ordinances, which the false apostles endeavored to impose upon them.<div eID="gen127538" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Col.2.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen127537" osisID="Col.2.20" type="section"/>
entries.14b9266cf07e75c98d0e6de4dc9c0741e7fe2afe: <div annotateRef="Bible:Col.2.21" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Col.2.21" sID="gen127540" type="section"/> <div sID="gen127541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">21. </hi><hi type="italic">Eat not, taste not.</hi> Hitherto this has been rendered — <hi type="italic">Handle not</hi>, but as another word immediately follows, which signifies the same thing, every one sees how cold and absurd were such a repetition. Farther, the verb <foreign xml:lang="el">ἅπτεσθαι</foreign> is employed by the Greeks, among its other significations, in the sense of <hi type="italic">eating</hi>, <note n="417"> <div sID="gen127542" type="x-p"/> An example occurs in Homer’s Odyssey, (6: 60,) <foreign xml:lang="el">σίτου θ ᾿ ἅπτεσθον καὶ χαρ́ετον</foreign>. — “Take food and rejoice.” See also Xenoph. Mem. 1. 3. 7. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen127542" type="x-p"/> </note> in accordance with the rendering that I have given. Plutarch makes use of it in the life of Caesar, when he relates that his soldiers, in destitution of all things, <hi type="italic">ate</hi> animals which they had not been accustomed previously to use as food. <note n="418"> <div sID="gen127543" type="x-p"/> “The passage referred to is as follows: — “ <foreign xml:lang="el">᾿Εβρώθη δὲ καὶ φλοιὸς ὡς λέγεται, καὶ ζώων ἀγεύστων πρότερον ἥ ψαντο</foreign>.” — “Even the bark of trees, it is said, was devoured, and they ate animals not previously tasted.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen127543" type="x-p"/> </note> And this arrangement is both in other respects natural and is also most in accordance with the connection of the passage; for Paul points out, (<foreign xml:lang="el">μιμητικῶς</foreign>,) <hi type="italic">by</hi> <hi type="italic">way</hi> <hi type="italic">of</hi> <hi type="italic">imitation</hi>, to what length the waywardness of those who bind consciences by their laws is wont to proceed. From the very commencement they are unduly rigorous: hence he sets out with their prohibition — not simply against eating, but even against slightly partaking. After they have obtained what they wish they go beyond that command, so that they afterwards declare it to be unlawful to taste of what they do not wish should be eaten. At length they make it criminal even to <hi type="italic">touch</hi>. In short, when persons have once taken upon them to tyrannize over men’s souls, there is no end of new laws being daily added to old ones, and new enactments starting up from time to time. How bright a mirror there is as to this in Popery! Hence Paul acts admirably well in admonishing us that human traditions are a labyrinth, in which consciences are more and more entangled; nay more, are snares, which from the beginning bind in such a way that in course of time they strangle in the end.<div eID="gen127541" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Col.2.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen127540" osisID="Col.2.21" type="section"/>
entries.369e28717aa469d96c79b7279663151207f58c6a: <div annotateRef="Bible:Col.2.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Col.2.22" sID="gen127544" type="section"/> <div sID="gen127545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22. </hi><hi type="italic">All which things tend to corruption.</hi> He sets aside, by a twofold argument, the enactments of which he has made mention — because they make religion consist in things outward and frail, which have no connection with the spiritual kingdom of God; and secondly, because they are from men, not from God. He combats the first argument, also, in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.14.17">Romans 14:17</reference>, when he says,<div eID="gen127545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen127546" type="x-p"/>The kingdom of God is not in meat and drink;<div eID="gen127546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen127547" type="x-p"/>likewise in <reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.6.13">1 Corinthians. 6 13</reference>,<div eID="gen127547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen127548" type="x-p"/>Meat for the belly, and the belly for meats: God will destroy both.<div eID="gen127548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen127549" type="x-p"/>Christ also himself says,<div eID="gen127549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen127550" type="x-p"/>Whatever entereth into the mouth defileth not the man, because it goes down into the belly, and is cast forth.<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.15.11">Matthew 15:11</reference>.)<div eID="gen127550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen127551" type="x-p"/>The sum is this — that the worship of God, true piety, and the holiness of Christians, do not consist in drink, and food, and clothing, which are things that are transient and liable to corruption, and perish by abuse. For abuse is properly applicable to those things which are corrupted by the use of them. Hence enactments are of no value in reference to those things which tend to excite scruples of conscience. But in Popery you would scarcely find any other holiness, than what consists in little observances of corruptible things.<div eID="gen127551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen127552" type="x-p"/>A <hi type="italic">second</hi> refutation is added <note n="419"> <div sID="gen127553" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Le second argument par lequel il refute telles ordonnances, est</foreign>;” — “The second argument by which he sets aside such enactments, is.”<div eID="gen127553" type="x-p"/> </note> — that they originated with men, and have not God as their Author; and by this thunderbolt he prostrates and swallows up all traditions of men. For why? This is Paul’s reasoning: “Those who bring consciences into bondage do injury to Christ, and make void his death. For whatever is of human invention does not bind conscience.”<div eID="gen127552" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Col.2.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen127544" osisID="Col.2.22" type="section"/>
entries.8c3287d5c05c6d204450633420b487c2388a0611:
23. Which have indeed a show. Here we have the anticipation of an objection, in which, while he concedes to his adversaries what they allege, he at the same time reckons it wholly worthless. For it is as though he had said, that he does not regard their having a show of wisdom. But show is placed in contrast with reality, for it is an appearance, as they commonly speak, which deceives by resemblance.
“Par similitude qu’elle ha auec la verite;” — “By the resemblance which it bears to the reality.”
Observe, however, of what colors this show consists, according to Paul. He makes mention of three — self-invented worship,
“Le seruice forgé a plaisir, c’est a dire inuenté par les hommes;” — “Worship contrived at pleasure, that is to say, invented by men.”
humility, and neglect of the body. Superstition among the Greeks receives the name of ἐθελοβρησκεία — the term which Paul here makes use of. He has, however, an eye to the etymology of the term, for ἐθελοβρησκεία literally denotes a voluntary service, which men choose for themselves at their own option, without authority from God. Human traditions, therefore, are agreeable to us on this account, that they are in accordance with our understanding, for any one will find in his own brain the first outlines of them. This is the first pretext.
The second is humility, inasmuch as obedience both to God and men is pretended, so that men do not refuse even unreasonable burdens.
“Iniques et dures a porter;” — “Unreasonable and hard to be borne.”
And for the most part traditions of this kind are of such a nature as to appear to be admirable exercises of humility.
They allure, also, by means of a third pretext, inasmuch as they seem to be of the greatest avail for the mortification of the flesh, while there is no sparing of the body. Paul, however, bids farewell to those disguises, for
what is in high esteem among men is often an abomination in the sight of God. (Luke 16:15.)
Farther, that is a treacherous obedience, and a perverse and sacrilegious humility, which transfers to men the authority of God; and neglect of the body is not of so great importance, as to be worthy to be set forth to admiration as the service of God.
Some one, however, will feel astonished, that Paul does not take more pains in pulling off those masks. I answer, that he on good grounds rests contented with the simple term show. For the principles which he had taken as opposed to this are incontrovertible — that the body is in Christ, and that, consequently, those do nothing but impose upon miserable men, who set before them shadows. Secondly, the spiritual kingdom of Christ is by no means taken up with frail and corruptible elements. Thirdly, by the death of Christ such observances were put an end to, that we might have no connection with them; and, fourthly, God is our only Lawgiver. (Isaiah 33:22.) Whatever may be brought forward on the other side, let it have ever so much splendor, is fleeting show.
Secondly, he reckoned it enough to admonish the Colossians, not to be deceived by the putting forth of empty things. There was no necessity for dwelling at greater length in reproving them. For it should be a settled point among all the pious, that the worship of God ought not to be measured according to our views; and that, consequently, any kind of service is not lawful, simply on the ground that it is agreeable to us. This, also, ought to be a commonly received point — that we owe to God such humility as to yield obedience simply to his commands, so as not to lean to our own understanding, etc., (Proverbs 3:5,) — and that the limit of humility towards men is this — that each one submit himself to others in love. Now, when they contend that the wantonness of the flesh is repressed by abstinence from meats, the answer is easy — that we must not therefore abstain from any particular food as being unclean, but must eat sparingly of what we do eat of, both in order that we may soberly and temperately make use of the gifts of God, and that we may not, impeded by too much food and drink, forget those things that are God’s. Hence it was enough to say that these
“Ces traditions;” — “These traditions.”
were masks, that the Colossians, being warned, might be on their guard against false pretexts.
Thus, at the present day, Papists are not in want of specious pretexts, by which to set forth their own laws, however they may be — some of them impious and tyrannical, and others of them silly and trifling. When, however, we have granted them everything, there remains, nevertheless, this refutation by Paul, which is of itself more than sufficient for dispelling all their smoky vapours;
“Tous les brouillars desquels ils taschent d’esblouir les yeux au poure monde;” — “All the mists by which they endeavor to blind the eyes of the poor world.”
not to say how far removed they
“Leurs traditions;” — “Their traditions.”
are from so honorable an appearance as that which Paul describes. The principal holiness of the Papacy,
“La premiere et la principale honnestete et sainctete de la Papaute;” — “The first and principal decency and sanctity of the Papacy.”
at the present day, consists in monkhood, and of what nature that is, I am ashamed and grieved to make mention, lest I should stir up so abominable an odour. Farther, it is of importance to consider here, how prone, nay, how forward the mind of man is to artificial modes of worship. For the Apostle here graphically describes
“Peind yci au vif;” — “Paints here to the life.”
the state of the old system of monkhood, which came into use a hundred years after his death, as though he had never spoken a word. The zeal of men, therefore, for superstition is surpassingly mad, which could not be restrained by so plain a declaration of God from breaking forth, as historical records testify.
Not in any honor. Honor means care, according to the usage of the Hebrew tongue. Honour widows, (1 Timothy 5:3,) that is, take care of them. Now Paul finds fault with this, that they
“Les traditions;” — “The traditions.”
teach to leave off care for the body. For as God forbids us to indulge the body unduly, so he commands that these be given it as much as is necessary for it. Hence Paul, in Romans 13:14, does not expressly condemn care for the flesh, but such as indulges lusts. Have no care, says he, for the flesh, to the gratifying of its lusts. What, then, does Paul point out as faulty in those traditions of which he treats? It is that they gave no honor to the body for the satisfying the flesh, that is, according to the measure of necessity. For satisfying here means a mediocrity, which restricts itself to the simple use of nature, and thus stands in opposition to pleasure and all superfluous delicacies; for nature is content with little. Hence, to refuse what it requires for sustaining the necessity of life, is not less at variance with piety, than it is inhuman.
CHAPTER 3
Colossians 3:1-4
1. If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God.
1. Ergo si consurrexistis cum Christo, quae sursum sunt quaerite, ubi Christus est in dextera Dei sedens:
2. Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.
2. Quae sursum sunt cogitate, non quae super terram.
3. For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.
3. Mortui enim estis, et vita nostra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo.
4. When Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory.
4. Ubi autem Christus apparuerit, vita vestra, tunc etiam vos cum ipso apparebitis in gloria.

So that it should seem best to retain <ns0:hi>hid</ns0:hi> as it is placed in the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> to this sense, <ns0:hi>q. d. In Christ are and dwell in the greatest fulness, all the treasures of wisedom, hid under the law, which are therefore called a mystery secret, or hidden thing from ages and generations, c.</ns0:hi> 1.26, 27. now made manifest to his Saints, they are now nor hid in Christ, but made known amongst the <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> as God willed: not then hidden riches, <ns0:hi>h. e.</ns0:hi> treasures of wisedom and knowledge of this mys<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tery as of hid treasure, but out of Christ, and before Christ amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi>: For Christ himself is that mystery, <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> 4.3. not hid after his appearance, but manifested, and manifesting the Father, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.18, however if any will rather choose to read, as if in Christ were at present hid all treasures, 'tis to be understood, stored up, not exposed to the view of every Eye, being as in a rich cabinet not to keep them from being known to men, but rather to make them more pretious and desireable.                <ns0:p n="4">4 And this I say <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Here he suggests the ground of his insisting upon the excellent treasures of the saving knowledge of Christ, and the ample description of him.</ns0:note>, lest any man should be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guile you <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">To this end that he might for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tifie them against delusion by paralogisms or sophistical and false reasonings, fallacious arguing (as the word notes, <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 1.22.) under a colourable pretence and shew of wisedom, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8, 18, 23.</ns0:note> with inticing words <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Set off with Rhetorical suasions and imbellish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments intimating the prevalency of such blandishments with fair words, and good speeches to seduce the simple (if the heart were not established with grace, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 16.18. & 4.14. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 5, 6. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.8, 9.) and therefore esteeming the excel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lent knowledge of Christ and being found in him, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 3.8, 9. they should beware of whatever under a shew of Religion is introduced to seduce them from the simplicity that is in Christ, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.3.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 For though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">To prevent any surmise that his distance at <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> might take him off from minding of them at <ns0:hi>Colosse,</ns0:hi> he shews that the great affection he bare to them did oblige him to inte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ress himself in all their concerns (the care of all the Church<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />es being incumbent on him, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.28.) and therefore that his bodily con<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>inement at <ns0:hi>Rome,</ns0:hi> did not hinder his pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sence with them in spirit. Not that we can conclude by some extraordinary operation of the Holy Ghost, God gave him now and then a clear prospect of what they did, as he did to <ns0:hi>Elisha</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Gehazi's</ns0:hi> behaviour, 2 <ns0:hi>K<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>g.</ns0:hi> 5.26. and of <ns0:hi>Eze<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kiel</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> of the secret actions of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Hierusa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lem</ns0:hi>; but that he was with them as with the <ns0:hi>Corinthians,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.3. when distant in body his thoughts and affections were exercised about them.</ns0:note>, joying and beholding your order <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">As it follows there as moving of fears lest they should be ensnared, so of joy understanding their <ns0:hi>order, i. e.</ns0:hi> their good Estate, constitution and consent in orderly walking and discipline, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 14.40. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 4.1. & 5.14.</ns0:note>, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">And the firmament of their faith in Christ, it being (if genuine) as firm as the firmament it self: stable as the Heavens and heavenly bodies, keeping their con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stant stations and regular courses and admitting nothing he<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terogeneous into them: all heavenly truths are as fixt Stars in this Orb, seeing all grace, because divine, hath an establishing property, so faith coming from the eternal moun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tains, All graces being connected in faith, which is a kind of firmament to them all, it comes to pass that faith in actuat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing any one grace, gives a strength, and further growth to every other grace.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> As ye have therefore received Christ Je<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sus the Lord <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Having caution'd them against sophistical seducers, and commended them for that order and sound faith he under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood to be amongst them, he here infers, an exhortation to continuance in both, especially in the latter with respect to the person of Christ according as he had before described him; for he doth not say as ye have received the <ns0:hi>doctrine</ns0:hi> of Christ or concerning Christ, but as <ns0:hi>ye have received Christ</ns0:hi> himself as, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.11, 12. & 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.11, 12. in whom is all treasured up for Salvation, he adds not onely <ns0:hi>Iesus</ns0:hi> (who came to save his people from their sins) but <ns0:hi>the Lord,</ns0:hi> intima<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mating they should not therefore suffer any rules of faith or life to be imposed upon them by any other whatsoever.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>so</ns0:hi> walk ye in him <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">But should be perswaded to abide in him whom they had embraced and order their conversation according to his mind, 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 4.1. knowing that he is the way, the truth, and the life, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 14.6. being led by his spirit, and deriving vertue to go on in this orderly walk and persevere in the faith.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:506" />7 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 2.21, 22. & 3.17.</ns0:note> Rooted and built up in him <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Shewing how they should abide and persevere in the faith, by continuing in him as branches do in the root, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 15.4. and resting upon him as a building upon the founda<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, <ns0:hi>Is.</ns0:hi> 28.16. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.11. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.22.</ns0:note>, and sta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />blished in the faith <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">And being firm and setled in the faith as, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 5.10. he adds this, not onely to clear the metaphorical expressions before, but to shew that they should be growing stronger as to the internal habit, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 92.13<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 14.</ns0:note>, as ye have been taught <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">He repeats as it were in a parenthesis (<ns0:hi>as ye have been taught</ns0:hi>) upon the matter, the same with as <ns0:hi>ye have received Christ</ns0:hi> in the former verse, for greater caution to them, who might be apt to have itching ears, that they should not be listening to any novel doctrines but abide in the faith of Christ.</ns0:note>, a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bounding therein with thanksgiving <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Setting down with themselves accor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ding to the superabounding grace they had, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 5.20. with 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.8. to abound, and increase therein, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.58. 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.8. having herein all the saving knowledge desireable without need of the addition of ought any other way; being thankfull to God that he had revealed such a Christ, his Christ to them; for they could not have a better, or another.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 16.17. Heb. 13.9.</ns0:note> Beware <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostle after his exhortation, considering their danger from seducing spirits lying in wait to deceive by their sleight and craftiness, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.1, 2. he doth here reinforce and enlarge his caution he had before suggested <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4. to engage to an heedfull avoidance of all seduction from Christ.</ns0:note> lest any man spoil you <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Lest their Souls should be made a prey, and they be carryed for a spoil by those worst of robbers that beset Christ's fold, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.20. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.13.</ns0:note> through philosophy <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">

'twas not really profitable.</ns0:note> and vain deceit <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">But a vain deceit or seduction, as seve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral take the next clause <ns0:hi>appositively</ns0:hi> and the conjunction <ns0:hi>ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />positively</ns0:hi>; yet if we consider what follows we may understand another general imposture, <ns0:hi>viz. superstition</ns0:hi> seeing <ns0:hi>vain de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceit after the tradition of Men,</ns0:hi> is so like that superstition our Saviour doth rebu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e in the Pharisees, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 15.9. seve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral branches of whic<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap> the Apostle doth afterward, in this Chapter dispute against, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 16. to 23. superstition might well be called <ns0:hi>deceit,</ns0:hi> from the cheat it puts upon Men, and the notation of the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word, which imports a withdrawing men from <ns0:hi>the way,</ns0:hi> Christ, and from <ns0:hi>his way</ns0:hi> of worship prescribed in his word: and <ns0:hi>vain</ns0:hi> it is as well as a deceit sith it is empty and unprofitable, not accompanied with God's blessing, nor conducing to the pleasing of him, but the pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />voking of him, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 106.29, 43.</ns0:note>, after the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Mat. 15.2.</ns0:note> tra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dition of men <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Being led by no other rule than the tradition of men, which is the same with the precepts of Men, <ns0:hi>Mar.</ns0:hi> 7, 8. which God likes not, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 8.20. & 28.13. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 20.31. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 26.22. 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.15, 16. he would not give place to humane traditions in his house.</ns0:note>, after the<ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or <ns0:hi>elements.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> rudiments of the world <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Nor to the <ns0:hi>Elements of the World</ns0:hi> (in allusion to <ns0:hi>Grammar</ns0:hi> wherein the Letters are the Elements or rudiments of all lite<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rature) <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> the Ceremonies of the Mosaical law, containing a kind of Elementary instruction, for that seems to be the A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postles meaning comparing this verse with the 20, and 21. of this Chapter and other places, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.24. these being but corporeal carnal and sensible ordinances suitable to a worldly sanctuary, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 9.1, 10. not to be imposed in that spiritual one which Christ hath set up, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 4.23, 24. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.2.</ns0:note>, and not after Christ <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Whatsoever Philosophical colours, or Pharisaical paint, they might appear in, they are not <ns0:hi>after Christ</ns0:hi>: we say a false Picture of a Man, is not after the man, being not ta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken from or resembling his person, but clean another; such descriptions of him, as were not taken from the life and truth that was in him.                      <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

               <ns0:p n="9">9 For <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The causal particle induceth this as an argument to en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />force the caution immediately foregoing against those who did seek to draw from Christ by Philosophy, as well as ur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ging the ceremonial law, else the Apostle's reasoning were not cogent unless against both.</ns0:note> in him <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">'<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>is evident that the Lord Jesus Christ, himself whom he had described and but just now named is the <ns0:hi>subject,</ns0:hi> the Person of whom he speaks, and in whom is seated and unto whom he attributes what followeth, <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> 1.19. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.14, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.16. he doth not say <ns0:hi>in his doctrine</ns0:hi> whatever <ns0:hi>Socinians</ns0:hi> cavill, as if they would render the Apostle absurd and not to agree with himself in what he asserts of Christ's Person before (as hath been shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed) and after in the context. 'Tis plain this relative <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> respects not onely, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8. but the 11<ns0:hi>th. &c.</ns0:hi> in whom the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieving <ns0:hi>Colossians</ns0:hi> are said to be compleat as their <ns0:hi>head,</ns0:hi> both in the former Chapter, and soon after in this: would it not be absurd to say, Christ's Doctrine is the head of Angels? we are crucified in the doctrine of Christ? buried and quic<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned together with his doctrine? the hand writing of ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nances was nailed to the Cross of doctrine? To silence all the Earth,</ns0:hi> that they should not restrain it to Christ's doctrine onely, what he asserts of his person, <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> after Christ had been se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veral years in Heaven, put it in the present tense.</ns0:note> dwelleth <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Dwelleth,</ns0:hi> not <ns0:hi>dwelt</ns0:hi> (as, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.5.) in regard of the person eternally the same, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.8. for his argument had not been cogent, to contain Christians in the faith of Christ, and their duty to him, to have alledged in the doctrine of Christ now in Heaven hath dwelt all the fulness of the God-head bodily (could propriety of speech have allowed it) but from the other respect because in their very flesh (the body of Christ now an inhabitant of the Heavens) the very Godhead in the whole fulness thereof personally from the moment of his incarnation doth yet dwell; what will no<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> the faithfull perform and work out with their utmost faith that they may never suffer themselves to be rent from spiri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tual and mystical union with him, in whom they understand that even they themselves shall be also divinely filled, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 10. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> in their measure be made partakers of the divine nature, 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.4. <ns0:hi>dwelleth</ns0:hi> imports more than a transient stay for a few minutes, or a little while, even abiding in him constantly and for ever (as dwelling most usually notes, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.16.)</ns0:note> all the fulness of the Godhead <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">That which doth thus perpetually abide in his person as denominated after the humane nature is <ns0:hi>all the fulness of the God-head, viz.</ns0:hi> That rich and incomprehensible abundance of perfections whereof the supream and adorable nature is full; so that indeed there is not at all any perfection, or ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cellency in the divine nature but is found abiding in him.                      <ns0:hi>Taken out of the way</ns0:hi> as the debt<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ors bond or obligation is, being cancell'd, and torn to pieces, so that there is no memorial or evidence of the debt doth re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />main, all matter of controversie being altogether remov'd. Yet (if it may be) to speak more fully and satisfactorily he annexeth.</ns0:note>, nailing it to his cross <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>And fasten'd it to his Cross,</ns0:hi> what could be more significant? implying that Christ by once offering himself a sacrifice on the Cross, had disarm'd the law, and taken away its condemning power, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 7.4. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.13. It being custo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mary (as learned men say) of old especially in <ns0:hi>Asia</ns0:hi> to pierce cancell'd obligations and antiquated writings with nails; Christ by his plenary satisfaction did not onely discharge from the condemnation of the law, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.1, 34. but he did effectually with the nails with which he himself was cru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cified by interpretation fasten the hand-writing of ordinances to his cross, and abolished the ceremonial law in every re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gard, since the substance of it was come and that which it tended to, was accomplished in giving himself a ransome for all, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2.6. to the putting away of sin, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 9.26. and obtaining eternal redemption, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 9.12.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="16">16 Let no man therefore judge you <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">He infers none should be condemned; none condemns ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther for exercising Christian liberty: none hath power to judge and censure herein, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> Suffer not any one (he excepts none) to impose upon you that, as necessary in the use and practice of it, which is not after Christ, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8. not warranted by his law of li<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />berty, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 14.3, 4. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.1. <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 1.25. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> himself would not be imposed on, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.12. & 7.23. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 2.5, 11.14. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> he would not (as one of the words doth note) be domineer'd over by any, or suffer any to exercise authority over him, who held the head and owned Christ to be Lord of the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />science, and sole Dictatour of what way he will be served in.</ns0:note>

               <ns0:p n="17">17 Which are a shadow of things to come <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Which as they were but obscurer representations or sha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dowy resemblances of future benefits procured by Christ, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 8.5. & 9.11. & 10.1. whatever temporary glory they had from the former institution, till the time of refor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mation, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 9, 10. yet that was done away, and they now had none, in respect of the glory that excelleth and remain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.9, 10.                   </ns0:note> beguile you ofyour re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">The original compound word peculiar in the <ns0:hi>N. T.</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> and that in this Epistle onely (and not very frequent in other Authours) hath occasioned interpreters here to ren<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der it variously, some joyning the next following word with it, and some (as we read it) to that which follows after. The simple word is, <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> 3.15. read <ns0:hi>rule,</ns0:hi> or judge, and it may be rendered <ns0:hi>intercede.</ns0:hi> Yet <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> doth not elsewhere use this word simply or in composition where he speaks of <ns0:hi>judging</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>condemning, Rom.</ns0:hi> 2.1. however it is borrow'd from those who were judges or umpires in their games, the Apostle most likely alluding to those who through favour or hatred determin'd unjustly, to the defrauding those victours of their prize or reward to whom it was due. Hence some would have the import to be agreeable to our translation; be carefull these unjust Arbiters do not defraud you of gain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Christ, and deceive you (as, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 24.4. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 5, 6. 2 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 2, 3.) by prescribing false lists and giving you wrong mea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sures, and so judging against you, one renders it, <ns0:hi>let no man deceive you with subtile argument</ns0:hi> who pleaseth or delights himself in humility; another, <ns0:hi>Let no man take your prize</ns0:hi>; others, <ns0:hi>Let no man Master it or bear rule over you at pleasure,</ns0:hi> Let none take upon himself, or <ns0:hi>usurp to himself the parts or office of a Governour or umpire over you.</ns0:hi> The Apostle labours to fortifie the true followers of Christ against such superstitious subtile ones who by their artifice did assume a magisterial au<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thority (without any sure warrant from God) to impose their traditionary and invented services upon them, and determine of their state accordingly as the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> do at this day. One learned man thinks the Apostle had not used this word here, but for some notable advantage, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> because the simple word may signifie to <ns0:hi>intercede</ns0:hi> as well as to <ns0:hi>judge,</ns0:hi> it made wonder<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fully to his purpose in this composition (as he uses <ns0:hi>concision, Phil.</ns0:hi> 3.2.) to disparage those seducers who did from some notions of the <ns0:hi>Platonists,</ns0:hi> labour to gain credit to that opi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nion that the Angels were intercessours betwixt God and Man.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Greek <ns0:hi>be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing a volun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />

                  </ns0:note> rudiments of the word <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Here the Apostle doth further argue against all impo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sitions of superstitious observances, obtruded as parts of di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine worship, whether in reviving those abrogated or serting up new ones<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> upon supposition of their union with Christ their head, and their being dead in him as to all beggarly Elements from which he had freed them by his death, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 6.3, 5. & 7.4, 6. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.9, 10, 11. with <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 2.19. no uncom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />manded worship or way of worship being <ns0:hi>after Christ,</ns0:hi> v. 8. <ns0:hi>in whom they were compleat,</ns0:hi> v. 11. <ns0:hi>being buried with him in Baptism,</ns0:hi> v. 12. <ns0:hi>having nailed those ritual ordinances to his Cross,</ns0:hi> as antiquated or out-dated, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14. why should they <ns0:hi>who held the head, v.</ns0:hi> 19.</ns0:note>: why as though living in the world are ye subject to ordinances <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">As if they lived in the old World with those Children in bondage, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.3. before Christ came, be subject to ceremonial observances, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> 'Tis most injurious that they should impose this yoke upon you, (<ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 15.10.) ye are most foolish if ye submit your necks: for God would not have a ceremonial worship which he himself instituted to be abrogated, that a new one should be invented by men. If the head of the Church like not the re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viving that worship he hath laid aside, be sure he will not ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prove of any new one which he never appointed. The A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postle is not here speaking of the Magistrates ordinances about things indifferent in their use for the real good of the civil Government; but of the way of worshipping God by Religi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous abstinencies, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Touch not, taste not, handle not <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which he doth here by way of imitation upbraiding of them, elegantly recite in the words, phrases, or sense of those imposing Dogmatists whose superstition and lust of do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mineering over the consciences of Christians is taxed in the gradation which the well skill'd in the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> judge to be in the original. For though the first and which we render <ns0:hi>touch not</ns0:hi> be sometimes so rendred, yet considering here the coincidency or tantology will, so rendred, make with the last, the sense of it, as the most judicious and learned have evi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />denc'd, seems to be, <ns0:hi>eat not,</ns0:hi> as noting they did forbid the eating, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> using certain meats at their ordinary meals (against the reviving of which imposition above, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 16. as well bring in a new one of like import the Apostle elsewhere expresseth himself, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 14.17. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.8. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.3.) obtaining which, they proceeded to forbid the not <ns0:hi>tasting,</ns0:hi> and then the not <ns0:hi>handling</ns0:hi> or touching of them with the hand, as if that would defile. It being more not to <ns0:hi>taste</ns0:hi> than not to <ns0:hi>eat,</ns0:hi> and likewise more not to <ns0:hi>touch with the finger,</ns0:hi> than not to taste. Expressing the ingeny of such superstitious im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posers, that they heap up one thing upon another to the bur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dening of consciences, not knowing where to make an end in their new invented external devotions and observances, which, as snares, do first bind fast, and in tract of time stran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gle. He speaks of these as distinct from those, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 16. they being for antiquated rites which had been of God's appoint<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, these for innovasions of man's invention as is apparent from the last verse.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:508" />22 Which all are to perish with the using <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">He adds his reasons why, under the Christian, institution acceptable worshipping of God doth not consist in such ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />servances, both because meats, drinks, garments, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> are designed unto the benefit of Man, for the preserving of his temporal life, and are consumed in their use. They cannot in, or by themselves either make a Man holy or render him unclean, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 15.11. <ns0:hi>Mar.</ns0:hi> 7.19. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 14.17. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.13. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.3. they all come to corruption or are consumed in doing us service, they cannot otherwise be of use, which may evince that all the benefit we receive from them doth onely respect this mortal life, it not being imaginable that what perisheth in our use should be of any force to the life of our Soul which is immortal and incorruptible. And therefore to urge the reviving of antiquated ordinances, or bringing in such like new ones, is to corrupt or consume the creatures without any spiritual advantage, whereupon such impositions must needs be destructive; and because of the Apostle's stronger argument, they are not after Christ, but <ns0:hi>after the precepts and decrees of men,</ns0:hi> compare <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8. which is our Lord and Masters argument against the innovations of the Pha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />resees, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 15.9. agreeing with the Prophet, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 29.13. to bring in additionals of uncommanded worship, or rites and ways of it, is forbidden of God, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 12.32. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 14.26. & 16.13. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 22.18. who (according to the purport of the second commandment, must be worshipped in a manner peculiar to him and appointed by him, and therefore wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship, not appointed, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> not commanded, is forbidden by him who will accept of no homage from Christians in the busi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of Religion, unless it be taught by him, and not by men onely.</ns0:note>) <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Tit. 1.14.</ns0:note> after the commandments and doctrines of men <ns0:hi>l.</ns0:hi>

(even as the Apostle doth by a compound word which signifies <ns0:hi>peace-making, c.</ns0:hi> 1.20. understand the very same thing which he expressed by the two simple words of which it is compounded, in another Epistle, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.15.) it being rational to conceive considering the Apostle's drift in the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />text that by <ns0:hi>will-worship</ns0:hi> he doth connote the same here, that by <ns0:hi>willing in worship,</ns0:hi> he doth assunder there.
